label: Analysis of algorithms
summary: Analysis of algorithms is the area of computer science concerned with determining the computational resources, chiefly running time and memory, required to execute an algorithm, typically as a function of the size of its input. It commonly characterizes efficiency using asymptotic notation such as big-O, and distinguishes worst-case, average-case, and best-case behavior. The systematic study of algorithmic efficiency is closely associated with Donald Knuth, whose multi-volume work The Art of Computer Programming helped establish the field, and it provides the analytical foundation for computational complexity theory and for comparing algorithms independently of particular machines.

label: Bounded rationality
summary: Bounded rationality is the idea that human decision-making is constrained by the difficulty of the problem, the cognitive capacity of the mind, and the time available, so that people typically settle for a satisfactory option rather than an optimal one. The term was coined by Herbert Simon as an alternative to the idealized rational-agent models built into expected-utility theory, and it has been used as a modeling basis across economics, political science, and related disciplines, not only within behavioral economics narrowly. Simon contrasted this satisficing approach with the classical assumption of unlimited computational and informational resources, and later researchers, including Gerd Gigerenzer, extended the concept by arguing that simple heuristics can outperform theoretically optimal procedures under real-world constraints. The concept remains actively used and debated across political science, economics, psychology, law, philosophy, and cognitive science.

label: Cell theory
summary: Cell theory holds that all living organisms are composed of cells, that the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in life, and that new cells arise only from pre-existing ones. The first two tenets are usually credited to Theodor Schwann and Matthias Jakob Schleiden in 1839, building on earlier microscopic observations by Robert Hooke and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, though Schleiden's own account of new cells forming by crystallization was later abandoned. Rudolf Virchow added the third tenet in 1855, though the underlying idea had already been proposed by Robert Remak. Some modern biologists continue to debate whether non-cellular entities such as viruses should count as living, since they are an exception to the theory's central claim.

label: Conservation of mass
summary: Conservation of mass is the principle that the total mass of a closed system remains unchanged over time, whatever internal processes act on it. Early experimental support is attributed to Jean Rey in the seventeenth century, and Mikhail Lomonosov articulated the law in 1756, but the more influential and widely credited demonstrations came from Antoine Lavoisier's later eighteenth-century experiments, which helped displace phlogiston theory and establish quantitative chemistry. The law holds only in the classical, non-relativistic regime; at very high energies or in systems with strong gravitational fields, mass and energy conservation must be treated jointly rather than separately.

label: Distinctive feature
summary: In linguistics, a distinctive feature is the most basic unit of phonological structure that distinguishes one sound from another within a language, such as the feature [+voice], which distinguishes the bilabial plosives [p] and [b]. Distinctive features are grouped into categories according to the natural classes of segments they describe: major class features, laryngeal features, manner features, and place features. The first distinctive feature theory was created by Russian linguist Roman Jakobson in 1941; features have traditionally been specified by binary values, an approach formally adopted in "Sound Pattern of English" by Noam Chomsky and Morris Halle in 1968.

label: Entropy
summary: Entropy is a thermodynamic state variable that quantifies the number of microscopic configurations, or microstates, consistent with a system's macroscopic condition. It is central to the second law of thermodynamics, which holds that the entropy of an isolated system left to evolve spontaneously cannot decrease over time, so such systems tend toward the state of highest entropy, or thermodynamic equilibrium. The concept originated in classical thermodynamics, where Rudolf Clausius defined it in 1865 as the ratio of an infinitesimal quantity of heat to temperature, and it was later given a statistical, microscopic foundation by Ludwig Boltzmann in terms of the possible arrangements of a system's atoms and molecules. Entropy is accordingly approached in two complementary ways: macroscopically, through classical thermodynamics, and microscopically, through statistical mechanics.

label: False consciousness
summary: False consciousness is a concept in the Marxist tradition referring to a systematically mistaken understanding of one's true social and economic situation, especially the way in which members of a subordinate class may hold beliefs that serve the interests of a dominant class rather than their own. Although the specific term is generally attributed to Friedrich Engels rather than to Karl Marx himself, it is closely associated with Marx's account of ideology and class, and it was developed by later Marxist theorists. It remains a discussed concept in sociology and social and political theory.

label: Generative grammar
summary: Generative grammar is an approach to the study of language, originating with the work of Noam Chomsky in the 1950s, that seeks to specify a finite system of explicit rules capable of generating all and only the grammatical sentences of a language. It treats grammar as a formal system representing the tacit linguistic knowledge, or competence, of an idealized native speaker, and is associated with the hypothesis of an innate universal grammar shared across human languages. The framework has passed through successive formulations, including transformational grammar, government-and-binding theory, and the Minimalist Program, and has been influential in linguistics and cognitive science while remaining contested among competing theoretical approaches.

label: Germ theory of disease
summary: Germ theory holds that microorganisms, or pathogens, cause infectious disease, and it displaced the earlier miasma theory that attributed illness to foul air. Basic versions of the idea were proposed by Girolamo Fracastoro in 1546 and elaborated by Marcus von Plenciz in 1762, well before either found scientific acceptance. A transitional period toward acceptance began in the late 1850s with Louis Pasteur's work on fermentation and spontaneous generation, and Robert Koch extended this work in the 1880s, including formulating criteria for linking specific microorganisms to specific diseases. By the end of the 1880s miasma theory was losing ground to germ theory among scientists, and a period of rapid bacteriological discovery followed.

label: Gödel numbering
summary: In mathematical logic, a Gödel numbering is a function that assigns to each symbol and well-formed formula of some formal language a unique natural number, called its Gödel number. Kurt Gödel developed the concept for the proof of his incompleteness theorems. It can be interpreted as an encoding in which a number is assigned to each symbol of a mathematical notation, so that sequences of symbols can be represented by natural numbers, facilitating their manipulation in formal theories of arithmetic. Since the publishing of Gödel's paper in 1931, the term has been used to refer to more general assignments of natural numbers to mathematical objects.

label: Ideal type
summary: The ideal type is a methodological construct developed by the sociologist Max Weber for use in comparative and interpretive social science. It is formed by selectively emphasizing certain features of a phenomenon and combining them into a unified analytical construct that does not correspond exactly to any single concrete case; Weber used the German word 'ideal' to mean the world of ideas rather than perfection or a statistical average. Because an ideal type is an admittedly artificial, one-sided construction, Weber held that its worth cannot be judged by how closely it corresponds to reality, only by its usefulness as an interpretive tool. Weber applied the method to build typologies, including four types of social action (zweckrational, wertrational, affektual, and traditional) and three ideal types of legitimate domination, using it to analyze both general phenomena, such as capitalism, and historically specific cases, such as the Protestant ethic.

label: Intentionality
summary: In philosophy, intentionality is the property of mental states of being about, directed at, or representing objects or states of affairs. The term in its modern sense was reintroduced by Franz Brentano, who treated directedness toward an object as the mark of the mental, and it was central to the phenomenology developed by Edmund Husserl, who made the analysis of intentional consciousness a core part of his method. Intentionality is a central topic in phenomenology and the philosophy of mind, where it figures in debates about mental representation and consciousness.

label: Internet
summary: The Internet is the global system of interconnected computer networks that communicate using the standardized Internet protocol suite (TCP/IP), linking devices and networks worldwide and carrying a broad range of information resources and services. It originated in packet-switching research of the 1960s and the ARPANET, funded by the U.S. Advanced Research Projects Agency, with the TCP/IP protocols developed in the 1970s enabling the interconnection of heterogeneous networks. The Internet is commonly distinguished from the World Wide Web, an information system of linked hypertext documents and other resources that runs over it. It underpins applications such as electronic mail, file transfer, and the Web, and its technical standards are coordinated by bodies including the Internet Engineering Task Force.

label: Invisible hand
summary: The "invisible hand" is a metaphor associated with the economist Adam Smith, used to describe how individuals pursuing their own self-interest in a market can unintentionally promote outcomes that benefit society as a whole. Smith used the phrase sparingly in his writings, including The Wealth of Nations, and it has since become a widely cited shorthand in economics for the idea that decentralized, self-interested exchange can produce socially beneficial coordination without central direction. It remains a foundational and much-discussed concept in economics, subject to varied interpretation.

label: Lambda calculus
summary: The lambda calculus is a formal system for expressing computation based on function abstraction and application, introduced by the logician Alonzo Church in the 1930s. Using a small set of rules for defining and applying functions, it provides a universal model of computation equivalent in power to the Turing machine, a correspondence expressed in the Church–Turing thesis. It is a foundational concept in computability theory and in the theory of programming languages, where it underlies functional programming.

label: Newton's law of universal gravitation
summary: Newton's law of universal gravitation describes gravity as a force by stating that every particle attracts every other particle in the universe with a force that is proportional to their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers of mass. It is a general physical law derived from empirical observations by what Isaac Newton called inductive reasoning; it is a part of classical mechanics and was formulated in Newton's Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica, first published on 5 July 1687. Its publication has become known as the "first great unification," marking the unification of gravity on Earth with known astronomical behaviors. The law was later superseded by Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity but continues to be used as an excellent approximation of the effects of gravity in most applications.

label: Logical positivism
summary: Logical positivism, also called logical empiricism, was a philosophical movement that flourished in the 1920s and 1930s, most prominently among members of the Vienna Circle and associated thinkers in Berlin. It combined empiricism with the tools of modern formal logic and held that meaningful statements are either analytic truths of logic and mathematics or empirically verifiable claims, treating metaphysical and much traditional philosophical discourse as cognitively meaningless on the strength of a verifiability criterion of meaning. Central figures included Moritz Schlick, Rudolf Carnap, and Otto Neurath, with A. J. Ayer helping popularize the view in the English-speaking world. The movement declined after the 1930s under internal difficulties with the verifiability criterion and external criticism, but strongly shaped the development of analytic philosophy and philosophy of science.

label: Mendelian inheritance
summary: Mendelian inheritance is the set of principles describing how discrete hereditary units — now identified with genes — are passed from parents to offspring, including the segregation of paired factors during reproduction and the independent assortment of different factors. These principles derive from the mid-nineteenth-century experiments of Gregor Mendel on pea plants, whose work was rediscovered around 1900 and became foundational to the science of genetics. Mendelian inheritance forms the classical basis of genetics, later extended and refined by the discovery of chromosomes, linkage, and molecular genetics.

label: Nash equilibrium
summary: A Nash equilibrium is a solution concept in game theory describing a set of strategies, one for each player, such that no player can improve their outcome by unilaterally changing strategy while the others keep theirs fixed. It was introduced by the mathematician John Nash in the early 1950s, who proved that such an equilibrium exists in a broad class of games. It is a central concept of non-cooperative game theory and is widely applied in economics, political science, and other fields that model strategic interaction.

label: Natural selection
summary: Natural selection is the process by which heritable traits that improve an organism's chances of survival and reproduction tend to become more common in a population over successive generations, while less advantageous traits become rarer. It was proposed as a principal mechanism of evolution by Charles Darwin (and independently by Alfred Russel Wallace) in the mid-nineteenth century and set out in detail in On the Origin of Species (1859). It is a central concept of evolutionary biology and, together with other mechanisms, accounts for the adaptation and diversification of living things.

label: Pragmatic maxim
summary: The pragmatic maxim, also known as the maxim of pragmatism or the maxim of pragmaticism, is a maxim of logic formulated by Charles Sanders Peirce. Serving as a normative recommendation or a regulative principle in the normative science of logic, its function is to guide the conduct of thought toward the achievement of its purpose, advising on an optimal way of "attaining clearness of apprehension." Peirce first stated it in 1878 in "How to Make Our Ideas Clear," advising that one should consider what conceivable practical effects the object of a conception might have, and that our conception of these effects is the whole of our conception of the object.

label: Probability Distribution
summary: A description of how probability is assigned across the possible values of a random variable.

label: Public-key cryptography
summary: Public-key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, is a class of cryptographic systems that use pairs of related keys, a public key that may be shared openly and a private key kept secret, so that operations performed with one key can only be reversed with the other. It enables secure communication and digital signatures without requiring the parties to share a secret key in advance, addressing the key-distribution problem of symmetric cryptography. The concept was introduced publicly by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in 1976, and the widely used RSA algorithm was described by Ronald Rivest, Adi Shamir, and Leonard Adleman shortly afterward; its security typically rests on computational problems such as integer factorization or discrete logarithms.

label: Random Variable
summary: A quantity whose value depends on the outcome of a random phenomenon.

label: Social fact
summary: A social fact is a concept introduced by the sociologist Émile Durkheim to denote ways of acting, thinking, and feeling that are external to individuals and exert a coercive influence over them, such as laws, customs, moral rules, and institutions. Durkheim argued that social facts are the proper subject matter of sociology and should be studied objectively, "as things," rather than reduced to individual psychology. The concept is foundational to sociology and to Durkheim's program for establishing it as an autonomous science.

label: Symbolic artificial intelligence
summary: Symbolic artificial intelligence is an approach to AI that represents knowledge using explicit symbols and rules and performs reasoning by manipulating these symbolic representations, for example through logic, search, and rule-based systems. It was the dominant paradigm of AI research from the mid-twentieth century into the 1980s, associated with early figures of the field such as those at the founding Dartmouth workshop, and includes expert systems and logic-based reasoning. It is often contrasted with connectionist and statistical machine-learning approaches, and remains a recognized subfield of artificial intelligence.

label: The unconscious
summary: In psychoanalysis, the unconscious is the part of the mind comprising mental processes — such as wishes, memories, and drives — that are not accessible to conscious awareness but are held to influence thought, emotion, and behavior. The concept was central to the psychoanalytic theory developed by Sigmund Freud, who held that unconscious material is kept from awareness by repression and can be inferred through phenomena such as dreams and slips. It is a foundational idea of psychoanalysis, though the notion of unconscious mental processes has a longer history and is understood differently across later psychology.

label: Tripartite classification of authority
summary: The tripartite classification of authority is Max Weber's typology of three ideal types of legitimate domination, which rarely appear in their pure form. It distinguishes charismatic authority, which grows out of the personal charm or strength of an individual personality; traditional authority, in which legitimacy comes from tradition or custom; and rational-legal authority, based on a system of rules applied administratively and judicially in accordance with known principles. The three forms are described as appearing in a hierarchical development order, with states progressing from charismatic through traditional to rational-legal authority, the form characteristic of a modern liberal democracy.

label: Turing machine
summary: A Turing machine is an abstract model of computation, introduced by Alan Turing in 1936, consisting of an infinite tape, a read/write head, and a finite set of states and rules that determine its behavior. Despite its simplicity, it can capture the notion of any effectively computable procedure, and it is used to make precise what it means for a function to be computable and for a problem to be decidable. It is a foundational concept of computability theory and theoretical computer science, closely associated with the Church–Turing thesis.

label: Uniformitarianism
summary: Uniformitarianism is the assumption that the natural laws and processes observed in the present have operated in the same way throughout the past and apply everywhere, underlying the geological maxim that the present is the key to the past. The idea originated with the geologist James Hutton in the late eighteenth century, was subsequently refined by John Playfair, and was popularized by Charles Lyell starting with his Principles of Geology in 1830; the term itself was coined by William Whewell in a review of Lyell's book. It was developed in opposition to catastrophism, which held that Earth's history was shaped mainly by sudden, large-scale upheavals. Many modern geologists no longer hold to a strict gradualist version of the idea, instead viewing Earth's history as a slow process punctuated by occasional catastrophic events.

label: Vector Space
summary: An algebraic structure of vectors closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

label: Will to power
summary: The will to power (German: der Wille zur Macht) is a concept in the philosophy of Friedrich Nietzsche that describes what Nietzsche may have believed to be the main driving force in humans. He never systematically defined it, leaving its interpretation open to debate. Broadly, his use of the term has been summarized as self-determination, the concept of actualizing one's will onto oneself or one's surroundings.

label: Arts and Design
summary: Creative disciplines spanning visual, performing, and applied arts and design.

label: Cognitive Sciences
summary: The interdisciplinary study of mind, cognition, and intelligent behavior.

label: Computer and Information Sciences
summary: The study of computation, information, and automated systems.

label: Engineering and Technology
summary: The application of scientific knowledge to design and build practical systems.

label: Formal Sciences
summary: Disciplines concerned with formal systems, such as logic, mathematics, and theoretical computer science.

label: Humanities
summary: The study of human culture, including philosophy, history, literature, and the arts.

label: Life Sciences
summary: The study of living organisms and life processes.

label: Medicine and Health
summary: The science and practice of preventing, diagnosing, and treating disease.

label: Meta-Knowledge
summary: Knowledge about knowledge: methodology, epistemology, and knowledge organization.

label: Natural Sciences
summary: The study of the physical world through observation and experiment.

label: Practical Knowledge
summary: Applied, skill-based, and craft knowledge oriented toward doing.

label: Social Sciences
summary: The study of human society and social relationships.

label: Aerospace Engineering
summary: Aerospace engineering is the primary field of engineering concerned with the development of aircraft and spacecraft. It has two major and overlapping branches, aeronautical engineering and astronautical engineering, while avionics engineering deals with the electronics side of the field. As an application of mechanical-engineering principles to flight vehicles, it draws on aerodynamics, propulsion, structures, and control. The Library of Congress Classification places aeronautics within range TL500-TL778, captioned "Aeronautics. Aeronautical engineering," inside the broader class TL1-TL4050, "Motor vehicles. Aeronautics. Astronautics." The American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, formed in 1963 by the merger of the American Rocket Society and the Institute of the Aerospace Sciences, is described as "the world's largest technical society dedicated to the global aerospace profession."

label: Alternative Medicine
summary: Alternative Medicine is the umbrella term for practices that aim to achieve the healing effects of medicine but that, by definition, lack biological plausibility, testability, repeatability, or supporting evidence of effectiveness, and are not part of evidence-based medicine. Such practices reside outside mainstream medicine and do not originate from the scientific method. Systems classified within it include homeopathy, chiropractic, and naturopathy.

label: Anesthesiology
summary: Anesthesiology, also spelled anaesthesiology or anaesthesia, is the medical specialty concerned with the total perioperative care of patients before, during, and after surgery. As a primary specialty it encompasses anesthesia, intensive care medicine, critical emergency medicine, and pain medicine.

label: Anthropology
summary: Anthropology is the social science that studies human beings, their societies, and their development. The American Anthropological Association, on its "What Is Anthropology?" resource, describes anthropology as "the study of what makes us human," explaining that to grasp "the full sweep and complexity of cultures across all of human history, anthropology draws and builds upon knowledge from the social and biological sciences as well as the humanities and physical sciences." The Association notes that "In the community of anthropologists in the United States, these four fields—human biology, archaeology, cultural anthropology, and linguistics—are understood to be the pillars on which the whole discipline rests," while observing that any individual anthropologist "will probably specialize in one or two of these areas but have general familiarity with them all." In the Library of Congress Classification the discipline occupies class GN, whose authority record carries the caption "Anthropology."

label: Archaeology
summary: Archaeology is the study of human activity through the recovery and analysis of material culture, including artifacts, architecture, biofacts, sites, and cultural landscapes. It can be considered both a social science and a branch of the humanities, and the discipline involves surveying, excavation, and eventually analysis of the data collected to learn more about the past.

label: Architecture
summary: Architecture is the study and practice of designing structures, especially habitable ones. It encompasses the process and the product of sketching, conceiving, planning, designing, and constructing buildings or other elements of the built environment, and it is widely treated as a discipline spanning both art and engineering. Although it utilizes civil engineering techniques, architecture is also considered a visual art, and architectural works are commonly recognized as cultural symbols and artistic expressions of their historical period. In the Library of Congress Classification, architecture occupies the schedule NA, "Architecture," within the fine arts. The profession is organized through bodies such as the American Institute of Architects, which describes itself as "the largest design organization in the world," working to transform the day-to-day practice of architecture toward a healthier and more equitable built environment.

label: Astronomy
summary: Astronomy is the natural science devoted to celestial objects and the phenomena that occur beyond Earth's atmosphere. The Encyclopaedia Britannica characterizes it as the "science that encompasses the study of all extraterrestrial objects and phenomena," adding that "since the late 19th century, astronomy has expanded to include astrophysics, the application of physical and chemical knowledge to an understanding of the nature of celestial objects." As a top-level field within the natural sciences, it studies bodies such as stars, planets, galaxies, and the interstellar and intergalactic medium, as well as the structure and evolution of the universe as a whole. Modern astronomy draws heavily on physics and chemistry through astrophysics, and on observational techniques spanning the electromagnetic spectrum and beyond. It is conventionally treated as a discipline distinct from, though closely allied with, physics and the other physical sciences.

label: Biology
summary: Biology is the scientific study of life and living organisms, the broad natural science encompassing the structure, function, growth, origin, evolution, and distribution of life. It is unified by fundamental themes: the cell as the basic unit of life, genes and heredity as the basis of inheritance, evolution as the driver of biological diversity, energy transformation sustaining life processes, and homeostasis. As the parent discipline of the life sciences, biology branches into specialized subfields organized around particular groups of organisms, levels of organization, or modes of study, including botany, zoology, microbiology, and systematics. In the Library of Congress Classification, the general literature of biology is gathered under class QH, ranging across periodicals, societies, and serial publications devoted to the science.

label: Biomedical Engineering
summary: Biomedical Engineering is the application of engineering principles and design concepts to medicine and biology for healthcare applications. It advances healthcare through diagnosis, monitoring, and therapy, and also encompasses the management of medical equipment in clinical settings. As an engineering discipline it is cross-listed into medicine.

label: Biotechnology
summary: Biotechnology is a multidisciplinary field that involves the integration of natural sciences and engineering sciences to achieve the application of organisms and parts thereof for products and services. Specialists in the field are known as biotechnologists. The discipline draws on biology, chemistry, and engineering to harness living systems, cells, and biomolecules in manufacturing and process development. Applications include the production of pharmaceuticals, enzymes, biofuels, and agricultural and food products, as well as industrial processes that use microorganisms or enzymes in place of conventional chemical synthesis. As an engineering and technology field, biotechnology emphasizes the design, scale-up, and control of biological processes to deliver marketable products and services, complementing the basic life sciences that supply its underlying knowledge.

label: Chemical Engineering
summary: Chemical engineering is an engineering field which deals with the study of the operation and design of chemical plants as well as methods of improving production. Practitioners develop practical commercial processes that transform raw materials into marketable products, integrating principles from chemistry, physics, mathematics, biology, and economics to manage energy and material transformations efficiently. Work ranges from small-scale laboratory study of nanomaterials to massive industrial operations. Core responsibilities include safety evaluations, process optimization, system modeling, reaction engineering, and operational guidelines for manufacturing facilities. The discipline is organized around unit operations and process design, scaling chemical and physical changes from the laboratory to continuous industrial production.

label: Chemistry
summary: Chemistry is one of the natural sciences, concerned with the substances that make up matter and the changes they undergo. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as "the science of the properties, composition, and structure of substances (defined as elements and compounds), the transformations they undergo, and the energy that is released or absorbed during these processes," noting that chemistry "is concerned with the properties of atoms and the laws governing their combinations." As a top-level field it serves as an umbrella over numerous specialized subfields, including analytical, inorganic, organic, and physical chemistry, as well as crystallography and electrochemistry, each addressing a distinct aspect of the composition, structure, reactivity, or measurement of chemical systems. Its central focus on atoms, molecules, and their transformations distinguishes it from neighboring natural-science fields while linking it closely to physics, the earth sciences, and the life sciences.

label: Civil Engineering
summary: Civil engineering is the engineering discipline concerned with the design, construction, and maintenance of the built environment and public infrastructure. The American Society of Civil Engineers describes civil engineers as professionals who "design, build, and maintain the foundation for our modern society – our buildings, roads and bridges, drinking water and energy systems, sea ports and airports, and the infrastructure for a cleaner environment." Practitioners typically specialize within the field, with recognized technical areas including structural, geotechnical, transportation, hydraulic, environmental, and construction engineering, as well as surveying. In the Library of Congress Classification, civil engineering is treated as a general engineering domain under the heading "Technology--Engineering (General). Civil engineering (General)." The field combines applied mechanics, materials science, and project management to deliver large-scale public works that serve communities over long operational lifespans.

label: Classics
summary: Classics, also known as classical studies, is the study of classical antiquity. In the Western world it traditionally refers to the study of ancient Greek and Roman literature and their original languages, Ancient Greek and Latin, and may also include Greco-Roman philosophy, history, archaeology, art, mythology, and society.

label: Computer Science
summary: The study of computation, algorithms, and information processing.

label: Dentistry
summary: Dentistry, also known as dental medicine and oral medicine, is the branch of medicine focused on the teeth, gums, and mouth. It consists of the study, diagnosis, prevention, management, and treatment of diseases, disorders, and conditions of the mouth, most commonly focused on dentition as well as the oral mucosa, and may also encompass other aspects of the craniofacial complex including the temporomandibular joint. The practitioner is called a dentist.

label: Dermatology
summary: Dermatology is the branch of medicine dealing with the skin, its structure, functions, diseases, and treatment. It is a medical specialty with both medical and surgical aspects.

label: Design
summary: Design is the discipline and practice of conceiving and planning objects, processes, and systems before they are made. A design is the concept or proposal for an intended artefact, and the verb to design names the process of developing it. A design is expected to satisfy goals and constraints within a specific context while accounting for aesthetic, functional, and experiential considerations. The field spans diverse domains, from architectural and engineering drawings and circuit diagrams to sewing patterns and less tangible artefacts such as business process models. In the Library of Congress Classification, design and the decorative and applied arts fall under class NK, captioned "Decorative arts. Applied arts. Decoration and ornament," reflecting the discipline's historical roots in ornament and craft as well as its modern role in shaping manufactured and communicated forms.

label: Earth Sciences
summary: The earth sciences form the top-level natural-science field concerned with the planet Earth as a physical system. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines them as "the fields of study concerned with the solid Earth, its waters, and the air that envelops it," noting that "included are the geologic, hydrologic, and atmospheric sciences" and that "their broad aim is to understand Earth's present features and past evolution and to use this knowledge to benefit humankind." As an umbrella field, the earth sciences encompass a range of specialized disciplines—among them geology, which studies the solid Earth, alongside the sciences of the oceans, fresh waters, and atmosphere. The field investigates Earth's composition, structure, processes, and history across spatial and temporal scales, and it connects closely with the other natural sciences, including chemistry and physics, through the study of materials, energy, and planetary processes.

label: Economics
summary: Economics is the social science concerned with the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services. The American Economic Association, a scholarly society in the field, describes economics on its student resources as "a broad discipline that helps us understand historical trends, interpret today's headlines, and make predictions about the coming years," noting that its study "ranges from the very small to the very large"—from microeconomics, "the study of individual decisions," to macroeconomics, "the study of the economy as a whole." The Association describes itself as "a nonprofit, nonpartisan, scholarly association with more than 17,000 members from academia, government, and business who are committed to the advancement of economics and its enduring contributions to society." In the Library of Congress Classification, economic theory falls within class HB, whose authority record bears the caption "Economic theory. Demography."

label: Education
summary: As an academic field, education is the scholarly discipline that studies teaching, learning, and the conditions under which they occur. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes education as "a discipline that is concerned with methods of teaching and learning in schools or school-like environments as opposed to various nonformal and informal means of socialization." The American Educational Research Association, a research society founded in 1916, describes itself as "a national research society" that "strives to advance knowledge about education, to encourage scholarly inquiry related to education, and to promote the use of research to improve education and serve the public good," and as "concerned with improving the educational process by encouraging scholarly inquiry related to education and evaluation." In the Library of Congress Classification, general works on education fall within class L, whose authority record carries the caption "Education (General)," with the theory and practice of education classed in LB.

label: Electrical Engineering
summary: Electrical engineering is an engineering discipline concerned with the study, design, and application of equipment, devices, and systems that use electricity, electronics, and electromagnetism. It emerged as an identifiable occupation in the latter half of the 19th century after the commercialization of the electric telegraph, the telephone, and electrical power generation, distribution, and use. The field is the parent discipline for a range of subfields, including telecommunications, computer engineering, power systems, control, signal processing, and photonics. Practitioners work across scales from microelectronic circuits and integrated devices to continent-spanning power grids and communication networks. In the Library of Congress Classification, electrical engineering, electronics, and nuclear engineering are grouped under class TK.

label: Emergency Medicine
summary: Emergency medicine is the medical specialty concerned with the care of illnesses or injuries requiring immediate medical attention. As a primary specialty its physicians provide care for unscheduled and undifferentiated patients of all ages and generally practice in hospital emergency departments, pre-hospital settings via emergency medical services, and intensive care units.

label: Environmental Engineering
summary: Environmental engineering is a professional engineering discipline related to environmental science. It encompasses broad scientific topics like chemistry, biology, ecology, geology, hydraulics, hydrology, microbiology, and mathematics to create solutions that will protect and also improve the health of living organisms and improve the quality of the environment. The field has historical roots in sanitary engineering and is regarded as a sub-discipline of civil engineering and chemical engineering. Typical work addresses water and wastewater treatment, air pollution control, solid and hazardous waste management, and the remediation of contaminated sites. Environmental engineers design systems and infrastructure that limit the discharge of pollutants and safeguard public health, distinguishing the discipline from environmental science, which centers on studying environmental processes rather than engineering solutions.

label: Environmental Science
summary: Environmental science is an interdisciplinary natural-science field that, in Encyclopaedia Britannica's words, is an "interdisciplinary academic field that draws on ecology, geology, meteorology, biology, chemistry, engineering, and physics to study environmental problems and human impacts on the environment." Nature Portfolio similarly defines it as "the multidisciplinary study of all aspects of the Earth's physical and biological environments," encompassing areas such as environmental chemistry, soil science, ecology, and climatology. The field is distinguished from environmental studies, which Britannica notes "emphasizes the human relationship with the environment and the social and political dimensions thereof." Classification systems place it among the natural sciences: the Universal Decimal Classification files "Environmental science. Conservation of natural resources. Threats to the environment and protection against them" within its main class 5, "MATHEMATICS. NATURAL SCIENCES." Together these sources frame environmental science as a bridging discipline that integrates multiple natural-science domains.

label: Family Medicine
summary: Family medicine is a medical specialty that provides continuing and comprehensive health care for the individual and family across all ages, sexes, diseases, and parts of the body. The specialist is usually a primary care physician called a family physician, and in certain countries family medicine is synonymous with general practice.

label: History
summary: History is the systematic study of the past, focusing primarily on the human past, and as an academic discipline it analyses and interprets evidence to construct narratives about what happened and explain why it happened. Some theorists categorize history as a social science, while others see it as part of the humanities or consider it a hybrid discipline. The term is also used more generally to mean the past itself rather than the academic field that studies it.

label: Human Geography
summary: Human geography is the social-science branch of geography that studies how people interact with places, focusing on the spatial relationships between human communities, cultures, economies, and their environments. It examines patterns such as urban sprawl and urban redevelopment using both qualitative and quantitative methods, drawing on sociology, anthropology, economics, and environmental science. Within the OECD's international classification of research fields, it falls under the social sciences as "Social and economic geography" (category 5.7). Geography as a whole is conventionally understood as a discipline bridging the social and natural sciences; human geography is the branch concerned with human activity and organization across space, complementary to physical geography. Its subfields include economic, cultural, political, population, and urban geography, each analyzing how social processes shape, and are shaped by, the spaces in which people live.

label: Industrial Engineering
summary: Industrial engineering is concerned with the design, improvement and installation of integrated systems of people, materials, information, equipment and energy. It draws upon specialized knowledge and skill in the mathematical, physical, and social sciences together with the principles and methods of engineering analysis and design, to specify, predict, and evaluate the results to be obtained from such systems. The branch focuses on optimizing complex processes, systems, and organizations by improving efficiency, productivity, and quality. Industrial engineers aim to reduce waste, streamline operations, and enhance overall performance across many industries; the Institute of Industrial and Systems Engineers notes that "Industrial and systems engineers make things better in any industry – from automobile manufacturing and aerospace, to healthcare, forestry, finance, leisure, and education."

label: Internal Medicine
summary: Internal medicine is a medical specialty focused on the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of diseases in adults. Also known as general medicine in Commonwealth nations, it concerns the internal organs, and many of its subspecialties (such as cardiology, nephrology, and endocrinology) address specific organ systems within adult medicine.

label: Law
summary: As an academic discipline, law is the field of scholarship concerned with legal rules, institutions, and reasoning. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes law as "the discipline and profession concerned with the customs, practices, and rules of conduct of a community that are recognized as binding by the community," noting that "Enforcement of the body of rules is through a controlling authority." The Association of American Law Schools, which describes itself as "a 501(c)(3) nonprofit association" of member law schools, states that it was "Founded in 1900" and that its mission "is to improve and advance legal education," pursued "by promoting the core values of excellence in teaching and scholarship, academic freedom, and diversity of viewpoints." In the Library of Congress Classification the discipline occupies class K, whose general authority record carries the caption "Law in general. Comparative and uniform law. Jurisprudence."

label: Library and Information Science
summary: Library and information science (LIS) is the field concerned with how society stores, retrieves, analyzes, manages, archives, and disseminates information, bridging the professional practice of librarianship with the scientific study of information. Members of the Association for Information Science and Technology (ASIS&T) — drawn from librarianship, linguistics, engineering, law, medicine, and other fields — share, in the association's words, "a common interest in improving the ways society stores, retrieves, analyzes, manages, archives and disseminates information." The Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology (JASIST), a fully refereed scholarly and technical periodical, has been published continuously since 1950 and publishes research and development in a wide range of subjects in information science and technology. The iSchools organization — an alliance of university schools and departments offering doctoral programs in the field — describes the discipline's scope as relying strongly on the social and behavioural sciences, computing, and linguistics, with topics including human-computer interaction, information organisation and access, and bibliometrics.

label: Linguistics
summary: Linguistics is the scientific study of language. The areas of linguistic analysis are syntax, semantics (meaning), morphology, phonetics, phonology, and pragmatics, and subdisciplines such as biolinguistics and psycholinguistics bridge many of these divisions.

label: Literary Studies
summary: Literary studies, also called literary criticism, is the study, evaluation, and interpretation of literature. It is closely related to literary theory, the philosophical analysis of literature's goals and methods, though the two activities are distinct and literary critics are not always theorists.

label: Materials Science and Engineering
summary: Materials science is an interdisciplinary field concerned with understanding the relationships between the structure of materials and their properties and using this knowledge to design materials for specific applications. The internal structure of a material—from atomic arrangements to microscopic features—strongly influences its mechanical, electrical, thermal, and optical behavior. In engineering practice, materials science and engineering are often described through the processing–structure–properties–performance paradigm, in which processing determines structure, structure determines properties, and properties ultimately control the performance of a material in service. The combined discipline therefore unites a scientific dimension, investigating why materials behave as they do, with an engineering dimension, producing and selecting materials for components and devices. Major material classes studied include metals, ceramics, polymers, semiconductors, and composites.

label: Mathematics
summary: The study of structure, quantity, space, and change.

label: Mechanical Engineering
summary: Mechanical engineering is an engineering branch concerned with physical machines and mechanisms involving force and movement. It combines engineering physics and mathematics with materials science to design, analyze, manufacture, and maintain mechanical systems, and is one of the oldest and broadest engineering branches. Core subject areas include mechanics, dynamics, thermodynamics, materials science, structural analysis, and design. The Library of Congress Classification places the discipline in range TJ1-TJ1570, captioned "Mechanical engineering and machinery." The American Society of Mechanical Engineers, founded in 1880, is the field's principal professional body; ASME states that its mission "is to advance engineering for the benefit of humanity."

label: Media and Communication Studies
summary: Media and communication studies is an academic discipline concerned with the content, history, institutions, and effects of communication and mass media, encompassing the study of how messages are produced, transmitted, and interpreted across interpersonal, organizational, and mass channels. The field draws on the social sciences and humanities, integrating theories from sociology, psychology, political science, cultural studies, and rhetoric, and examines print, broadcast, film, and digital media. It emerged as a distinct academic area over the twentieth century and includes subfields such as mass communication, media effects research, and cultural and critical media studies.

label: Medical Physics
summary: Medical physics deals with the application of the concepts and methods of physics to the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of human diseases, with a specific goal of improving human health and well-being. Since 2008 it has been included as a health profession according to the International Standard Classification of Occupations of the International Labour Organization.

label: Music
summary: Music is studied and practiced as an academic discipline in university music departments and conservatories, encompassing performance, composition, and the scholarly study of music. In the Library of Congress Classification, music occupies Class M, organized as "Music and Books on Music," with literature on music in Class ML and instruction and study in Class MT. As a field, music spans creative activities commonly divided into composition, improvisation, and performance, and its scholarly branches include musicology, music theory, ethnomusicology, and music education. The American Musicological Society, founded in 1934, was "crucial in legitimizing musicology as a scholarly discipline," reflecting music's establishment as a research field alongside its conservatory training traditions in performance and pedagogy.

label: Neurology
summary: Neurology is the branch of medicine dealing with the diagnosis and treatment of conditions and diseases involving the nervous system, which comprises the brain, the spinal cord, and the peripheral nerves. It is a medical specialty that draws on the field of neuroscience.

label: Neuroscience
summary: Neuroscience is the scientific study of the nervous system, its functions, and its disorders. It is a multidisciplinary science that combines physiology, anatomy, molecular biology, developmental biology, cytology, psychology, physics, computer science, chemistry, medicine, statistics, and mathematical modeling to understand the properties of neurons, glia, and neural circuits, drawing together the biological, physical, computational, and behavioral sciences in the study of the brain and nervous system.

label: Nursing
summary: Nursing is a health care profession that integrates the art and science of caring and focuses on the protection, promotion, and optimization of health and human functioning, the prevention of illness and injury, the facilitation of healing, and the alleviation of suffering. It is one of the principal allied health professions within health care.

label: Obstetrics and Gynaecology
summary: Obstetrics and gynaecology is the medical specialty that encompasses the two subspecialties of obstetrics and gynaecology. Obstetrics is concerned with the management and care of women during pregnancy, parturition, and the puerperium, while gynaecology is concerned primarily with disorders of the female genital tract and reproductive physiology.

label: Ophthalmology
summary: Ophthalmology is the branch of medicine that deals with the diagnosis, treatment, and surgery of eye diseases and disorders. It is a surgical specialty concerned with the structure and function of the eye and the medical and surgical treatment of its defects and diseases.

label: Otolaryngology
summary: Otorhinolaryngology, commonly known as otolaryngology or ENT, is a surgical subspecialty within medicine that deals with the surgical and medical management of conditions of the head and neck. It is concerned with the study and treatment of disorders of the ear, nose, and throat.

label: Pathology
summary: Pathology is the study of disease and a significant field in modern medical diagnosis and medical research. In contemporary medicine the term refers to the diagnostic specialty of general pathology, which encompasses inter-related specialties that diagnose disease mostly through analysis of tissue and human cell samples. A physician practicing pathology is called a pathologist.

label: Pediatrics
summary: Pediatrics is the branch of medicine that involves the medical care of infants, toddlers, children, adolescents, and young adults. It is a medical specialty concerned with maintaining health and providing care to children from birth to adolescence.

label: Performing Arts
summary: The performing arts are arts performed for an audience, encompassing disciplines presented before a live audience including theatre, music, and dance. They are distinguished from the visual arts, which produce physical or static objects rather than a transient performance enacted in real time. As a field of study and practice, the performing arts treat the human body, voice, and movement as the primary medium, and the live encounter between performer and spectator as constitutive of the work. Allied performance forms include opera, mime, circus arts, spoken word, and puppetry. In the Library of Congress Classification, dramatic and theatrical performance falls under the range PN2000-PN3307, "Dramatic representation. The theater," within the broader Language and Literature schedule, while music and dance are classed separately under M and GV respectively.

label: Pharmacology
summary: Pharmacology is the science of drugs and medications, including a substance's origin, composition and interaction with biological systems, specifically through pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, therapeutic use, and toxicology. It examines how a substance alters normal or abnormal biochemical function. As a branch of biomedical science it is distinct from pharmacy, the clinical profession of preparing and dispensing medicines.

label: Pharmacy
summary: Pharmacy is the science and practice of discovering, producing, preparing, dispensing, reviewing and monitoring medications, aiming to ensure the safe, effective, and affordable use of medicines. It links health sciences with pharmaceutical sciences and natural sciences. Based on the setting, pharmacy practice is classified as either community or institutional pharmacy, and providing direct patient care in these settings is considered clinical pharmacy.

label: Philosophy
summary: Philosophy is an academic discipline that examines fundamental questions about existence, knowledge, value, reason, and language through systematic argument and analysis. Its major branches include metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, logic, and aesthetics, among others. The discipline traces its recorded origins to ancient Greece, though philosophical traditions developed independently across many cultures.

label: Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
summary: Physical medicine and rehabilitation (PM&R), also known as physiatry and, outside the United States, as physical and rehabilitation medicine, is a branch of medicine that aims to enhance and restore functional ability and quality of life to people with physical impairments or disabilities. PM&R physicians lead rehabilitation teams in inpatient and outpatient settings and are trained in medication management, electrodiagnosis, and targeted injections.

label: Physics
summary: The study of matter, energy, and the fundamental forces of nature.

label: Political Science
summary: Political science is the social science concerned with the study of government, politics, and power. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as "the systematic study of governance by the application of empirical and generally scientific methods of analysis," adding that "As traditionally defined and studied, political science examines the state and its organs and institutions." The American Political Science Association, founded in 1903, describes itself as bringing "together political scientists from all fields of inquiry, regions, and occupational endeavors within and outside academe to deepen our understanding of politics, democracy, and citizenship throughout the world." In the Library of Congress Classification the discipline's general works fall within class JA, whose authority record carries the caption "Political science (General)."

label: Psychiatry
summary: Psychiatry is the medical specialty devoted to the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of mental disorders, including conditions related to cognition, perception, mood, emotion, and behavior. It is recognized as a primary medical specialty.

label: Psychology
summary: Psychology is the scientific study of the mind and behavior, with subject matter that includes the behavior of humans and nonhumans, conscious and unconscious phenomena, and mental processes such as thoughts, feelings, and motives. It is "an academic discipline of broad scope, crossing the boundaries between the natural and social sciences," linking to neuroscience through biological psychology while also functioning as a social science aimed at understanding the behavior of individuals and groups.

label: Public Health
summary: Public health is the science of preventing disease, prolonging life, and promoting health through organized efforts and informed choices of society, organizations, communities, and individuals. Its scope spans populations ranging from small groups to entire cities or, in the case of a pandemic, several continents. Analyzing the determinants of health of a population and the threats it faces forms the basis of the field.

label: Radiology
summary: Radiology is the medical specialty that uses medical imaging to diagnose diseases and guide treatment within the bodies of humans and other animals. It began with radiography but today includes imaging modalities that use no ionizing radiation, such as ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging, as well as those that do, such as computed tomography, fluoroscopy, and nuclear medicine. Interventional radiology is the performance of usually minimally invasive medical procedures with the guidance of these imaging technologies.

label: Religious Studies
summary: Religious studies is the study of religion from a historical or scientific perspective, approaching it empirically rather than from within any faith tradition. The discipline describes, compares, interprets, and explains religion, emphasizing empirical, historically based, and cross-cultural perspectives.

label: Sociology
summary: Sociology is the social science that studies human society and social behavior. The American Sociological Association, on its "What Is Sociology?" resource, defines it as "the study of social life, social change, and the social causes and consequences of human behavior," explaining that "Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations, and societies and how people interact within these contexts," so that "the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities." The Association describes itself as having been "founded in 1905" and as "the national professional membership association for sociologists and others who are interested in sociology," with a mission to "advance sociology as a science and profession, and promote the contributions and use of sociology to society." In the Library of Congress Classification the discipline occupies class HM, whose authority record carries the caption "Sociology."

label: Statistics
summary: The discipline of collecting, analyzing, and interpreting data under uncertainty.

label: Surgery
summary: Surgery is a medical specialty that uses manual and instrumental techniques to diagnose or treat pathological conditions, to alter bodily functions, to reconstruct or alter aesthetics and appearance, or to remove unwanted tissues, neoplasms, and foreign bodies. As a primary specialty it serves as the parent field for numerous procedural subspecialties.

label: Systems Science
summary: Systems science is an interdisciplinary field devoted to the study of complex systems—their structure, behavior, and the principles that govern them across domains that do not fit neatly within a single traditional discipline. The International Society for the Systems Sciences (ISSS), founded in 1954, is one of the oldest organizations dedicated to advancing systems science, cybernetics, and complexity science, and characterizes the field as addressing transdisciplinary problems such as climate change, artificial intelligence, and economic systems. The field draws on mathematics, engineering, biology, and the social sciences to develop general frameworks applicable wherever components interact to produce emergent system-level behavior.

label: Visual Arts
summary: The visual arts are art forms perceived primarily through sight, encompassing painting, drawing, printmaking, sculpture, ceramics, photography, video, filmmaking, design, crafts, and architecture. The field also takes in the applied arts—industrial design, graphic design, fashion design, interior design, and decorative art—alongside disciplines such as performing arts and textile arts that involve visual aspects among other dimensions. In the Library of Congress Classification, the visual arts fall under the broad Fine Arts class N, where subdivisions span history, museums and galleries, and the individual media. The category groups practices that share a basis in the making and study of visual objects and images, distinguishing them from the literary and musical arts.

label: Vienna Circle
summary: The Vienna Circle (German: Wiener Kreis) was a group of philosophers, scientists, and mathematicians who met in Vienna from the 1920s until the mid-1930s, gathering around the philosopher Moritz Schlick, and was the principal center of the movement known as logical positivism or logical empiricism. Its members and associates, who included Rudolf Carnap, Otto Neurath, Hans Hahn, and (more loosely) figures such as Kurt Gödel, sought to develop a scientifically grounded philosophy using modern logic and to eliminate metaphysics, a program set out in the 1929 manifesto commonly titled The Scientific Conception of the World. The Circle dispersed in the 1930s amid the political upheaval of the period and the assassination of Schlick in 1936, with many members emigrating and carrying its influence into analytic philosophy and philosophy of science abroad.

label: Bayesian Inference
summary: A method of statistical inference that updates probabilities as evidence is acquired.

label: Gradient Descent
summary: An iterative optimization method that updates parameters in the direction that most reduces a function's value.

label: Adam Smith
summary: Adam Smith (1723–1790) was a Scottish economist and philosopher, a pioneer in the field of political economy and a key figure during the Scottish Enlightenment who is widely seen as the "father of economics." He is best known for An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776), regarded as marking the inception of modern economic scholarship as a comprehensive system and an academic discipline. In it he laid the foundational principles of classical free-market economic theory, developing the concept of division of labour and explaining how rational self-interest and competition can lead to economic prosperity.

label: Alan Turing
summary: Alan Turing (1912–1954) was a British mathematician and logician widely regarded as a founder of computability theory and a pioneer of theoretical computer science. In his 1936 paper "On Computable Numbers," he introduced the abstract computing device now known as the Turing machine and used it to address the Entscheidungsproblem, establishing a formal notion of what it means for a function to be effectively computable. His ideas about machine intelligence, including the test later named after him, were also influential in the philosophy of mind.

label: Alfred Russel Wallace
summary: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913) was an English naturalist, explorer, and biologist who independently conceived the theory of evolution through natural selection, his 1858 paper being published alongside extracts from Charles Darwin's writings. Through extensive fieldwork in the Amazon basin and the Malay Archipelago, he studied the geographical distribution of animal species, identifying the faunal divide now termed the Wallace Line and becoming known as a founding figure of biogeography. He was regarded as one of the leading evolutionary thinkers of the 19th century, working on warning coloration and reinforcement, and remained a prolific writer on both scientific and social questions.

label: Alfred Tarski
summary: Alfred Tarski (1901–1983) was a Polish-American logician and mathematician best known for his work on model theory, metamathematics, and algebraic logic. Educated at the University of Warsaw and a member of the Lwów–Warsaw school of logic, he immigrated to the United States in 1939 and carried out research at the University of California, Berkeley, from 1942 until his death. His biographers state that, along with his contemporary Kurt Gödel, he changed the face of logic in the twentieth century, especially through his work on the concept of truth and the theory of models.

label: Allen Newell
summary: Allen Newell (1927–1992) was an American computer scientist and cognitive psychologist who worked at the RAND Corporation before moving to Carnegie Mellon University. With Herbert A. Simon and programmer Cliff Shaw, he built the Information Processing Language and, in 1956, the Logic Theorist — one of the earliest artificial intelligence programs — followed the next year by the General Problem Solver; his contributions to those programs are credited with helping establish artificial intelligence as a field. Newell and Simon went on to formulate the physical symbol system hypothesis — that intelligent behavior in general amounts to symbol manipulation of the sort their own programs performed — and in 1975 the two shared the ACM Turing Award for their contributions to artificial intelligence and the psychology of human cognition.

label: Alonzo Church
summary: Alonzo Church (1903–1995) was an American mathematician, logician, and philosopher who made major contributions to mathematical logic and the foundations of theoretical computer science. He is best known for the lambda calculus, the Church–Turing thesis, and his proof of the unsolvability of the Entscheidungsproblem. Alongside his doctoral student Alan Turing, Church is considered one of the founders of computer science, and the lambda calculus later became foundational to the study of programming languages.

label: Amartya Sen
summary: Amartya Sen (born 1933) is an Indian economist and philosopher widely recognized for his contributions to welfare economics and social choice theory. In 1998 he received the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for his contributions to welfare economics, and he has also made major contributions to social choice theory, development economics, and the measurement of well-being. He is the Thomas W. Lamont University Professor and professor of economics and philosophy at Harvard University, and in 1999 received India's highest civilian honour, the Bharat Ratna.

label: Amos Tversky
summary: Amos Tversky (1937–1996) was an Israeli cognitive and mathematical psychologist and a key figure in the discovery of systematic human cognitive bias and the handling of risk. His early work with Daniel Kahneman focused on the psychology of prediction and probability judgment, and together they developed prospect theory, considered one of the seminal works of behavioral economics that aims to explain irrational human economic choices. Six years after Tversky's death, Kahneman received the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for work done in collaboration with him.

label: Andreas Vesalius
summary: Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564) was an anatomist and physician, often referred to as the founder of modern human anatomy. He wrote De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem, considered one of the most influential books on human anatomy and a major advance over the long-dominant work of Galen. Born in Brussels, he was a professor at the University of Padua and later became Imperial physician at the court of Emperor Charles V.

label: Andrey Kolmogorov
summary: Andrey Kolmogorov (1903–1987) was a Soviet mathematician who played a central role in the creation of modern probability theory. He also gave fundamental contributions to the mathematics of topology, intuitionistic logic, turbulence, classical mechanics, functional analysis, algorithmic information theory, and computational complexity. His work is widely regarded as foundational to the formalization of probability as a mathematical discipline.

label: Antoine Lavoisier
summary: Antoine Lavoisier (1743–1794) was a French chemist central to the 18th-century chemical revolution, whose work had a large influence on both the history of chemistry and the history of biology. He is noted for his discovery of the role oxygen plays in combustion, opposing the prior phlogiston theory, and for confirming the law of conservation of mass through precise quantitative measurement. He set out his reforms in the Traité élémentaire de chimie, wrote the first extensive list of elements, and helped reform chemical nomenclature.

label: Arthur Schopenhauer
summary: Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) was a German philosopher and writer, best known for his 1818 work The World as Will and Representation, which characterizes the phenomenal world as the manifestation of a blind and irrational noumenal will. Building on the transcendental idealism of Immanuel Kant, he developed an atheistic metaphysical and ethical system whose work has been described as an exemplary manifestation of philosophical pessimism. His writing on aesthetics, morality, and psychology had a posthumous impact across disciplines and influenced many thinkers and artists.

label: Auguste Comte
aliases: Isidore Auguste Marie François Xavier Comte
summary: Auguste Comte (1798–1857) was a French philosopher and writer who formulated the doctrine of positivism and is often regarded as the first philosopher of science in the modern sense. His ideas were fundamental to the development of sociology, a discipline whose very term he invented and which he treated as the crowning achievement of the sciences. His concept of sociology set the tone for early social theorists, evolving into the modern academic sociology presented by Émile Durkheim.

label: Bertrand Russell
summary: Bertrand Russell (1872–1970) was an English philosopher, logician, and mathematician regarded as a founder of analytic philosophy, along with his predecessor Gottlob Frege, his colleague G. E. Moore, and his student Ludwig Wittgenstein. Together with his former teacher Alfred North Whitehead, he wrote Principia Mathematica, a major attempt to reduce the whole of mathematics to logic. His work in logic and the foundations of mathematics later influenced the development of computer science.

label: Carl Friedrich Gauss
summary: Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855) was a German mathematician, astronomer, geodesist, and physicist whose foundational contributions to number theory are set out in his masterpiece Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, including the law of quadratic reciprocity. His work reached across algebra, analysis, geometry, statistics, and probability, and he introduced concepts such as Gaussian curvature and the method of least squares. He led the geodetic survey of the Kingdom of Hanover and was one of the founders of geophysics, connecting his mathematics to geodesy and the study of Earth's magnetic field.

label: Carl Linnaeus
summary: Carl Linnaeus (1707–1778) was a Swedish biologist and physician widely regarded as a founder of modern biological systematics, remembered as the "father of modern taxonomy" for formalizing binomial nomenclature, the modern system of naming organisms. He set out this system in his Systema Naturae, first published in the Netherlands in 1735, and spent subsequent decades collecting and classifying plants, animals, and minerals. His conventions for naming species remain foundational to biology, and he is also considered one of the founders of modern ecology.

label: Cesare Beccaria
summary: Cesare Beccaria (1738–1794) was an Italian criminologist, jurist, philosopher, and economist best remembered for his 1764 treatise On Crimes and Punishments, which condemned torture and the death penalty. That work was a founding contribution to penology and the classical school of criminology, and Beccaria is considered the father of modern criminal law and of criminal justice. According to John Bessler, his works had a profound influence on the Founding Fathers of the United States.

label: Charles Darwin
summary: Charles Darwin (1809–1882) was a British naturalist widely regarded as the founder of evolutionary biology, best known for proposing that species evolve over generations through the process of natural selection. He set out this theory with extensive evidence in On the Origin of Species (1859), drawing on observations from his voyage on HMS Beagle and decades of subsequent study. His work reshaped the biological sciences and has also been cited as an influence on fields such as evolutionary psychology.

label: Charles Lyell
summary: Charles Lyell (1797–1875) was a Scottish geologist who demonstrated the power of known natural causes in explaining the earth's history. He is best known as the author of Principles of Geology (1830–33), which presented to a wide public audience the idea that the earth was shaped by the same natural processes still in operation today, a gradualistic view later dubbed "uniformitarianism." A close friend of Charles Darwin, he contributed significantly to Darwin's thinking on the processes involved in evolution.

label: Charles Sanders Peirce
summary: Charles Sanders Peirce (1839–1914) was an American scientist, mathematician, logician, and philosopher widely regarded as a founder of pragmatism and, independently of Ferdinand de Saussure, of semiotics, the study of signs. Trained as a chemist and employed as a scientist for thirty years, he made major contributions to logic, including theories of relations and quantification, and formulated the pragmatic maxim at the heart of pragmatist thought. He saw logic as the formal branch of semiotics, of which he is a founder, developing a sign theory that foreshadowed later debates in the philosophy of language.

label: Charles Spearman
summary: Charles Spearman (1863–1945) was an English psychologist known for his work in statistics, as a pioneer of factor analysis, and for Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. He did seminal work on models for human intelligence, including his theory that disparate cognitive test scores reflect a single general intelligence factor, for which he coined the term g factor. His statistical approach to mental measurement is foundational to the field of psychometrics.

label: Claude Lévi-Strauss
summary: Claude Lévi-Strauss (1908–2009) was a French anthropologist widely regarded as the founder of structural anthropology, an approach that analyzes culture — including myth, kinship, and classification — as systems of underlying structures modeled on the relational logic of structural linguistics. Drawing on the linguistics of Ferdinand de Saussure and Roman Jakobson, he set out this program in works such as The Elementary Structures of Kinship and Structural Anthropology. His methods were highly influential across the social sciences and the humanities, including literary theory.

label: Claude Shannon
summary: Claude Shannon (1916–2001) was an American mathematician, electrical engineer, and cryptographer known as the "father of information theory" and the man who laid the foundations of the Information Age. His 1948 paper "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" laid the foundations for the field of information theory, and his earlier work was the first to describe the use of Boolean algebra as essential to digital electronic circuits. His theory has been applied across many disciplines, and its formal treatment of communication became foundational to fields such as computational linguistics.

label: Daniel Kahneman
summary: Daniel Kahneman (1934–2024) was an Israeli-American psychologist widely regarded as a founder of behavioral economics and best known for his work on the psychology of judgment and decision-making, for which he was awarded the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences together with Vernon L. Smith. Working with Amos Tversky and others, he established a cognitive basis for common human errors arising from heuristics and biases and developed prospect theory, findings that challenged the assumption of human rationality in modern economic theory. His 2011 book Thinking, Fast and Slow summarized much of this research and became a best seller.

label: David Deutsch
summary: David Deutsch (born 1953) is a British physicist at the University of Oxford who is often described as the "father of quantum computing". He pioneered the field of quantum computation by formulating a description for a quantum Turing machine, as well as specifying an algorithm designed to run on a quantum computer. He is a visiting professor at the Centre for Quantum Computation in the Clarendon Laboratory of the University of Oxford and a proponent of the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics.

label: David Hilbert
summary: David Hilbert (1862–1943) was a German mathematician and philosopher of mathematics widely regarded as a co-founder of proof theory and mathematical logic, and one of the most influential mathematicians of all time.
