He discovered and developed a broad range of fundamental ideas, including invariant theory, the foundations of geometry, and the foundations of mathematics, and in 1900 presented a collection of problems that set a course for mathematical research of the 20th century. He adopted and defended Georg Cantor's set theory and transfinite numbers, helping establish the rigorous foundations on which modern logic was built.

label: Donald Knuth
summary: Donald Knuth is an American computer scientist widely credited with helping to establish the analysis of algorithms as a rigorous area of computer science, principally through his multi-volume work The Art of Computer Programming. He is also known for creating the TeX typesetting system and for foundational contributions to the theory and mathematical analysis of algorithms. His work is commonly regarded as central to the development of computer science as a mathematical discipline.

label: Duncan Black
summary: Duncan Black (1908–1991) was a Scottish economist who laid the foundations of social choice theory and public choice. He was responsible for unearthing the work of many early political scientists, including Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, and devised the Black electoral system, a Condorcet method in which the Borda winner is chosen in the absence of a Condorcet winner. His work is regarded as foundational to the formal study of collective decision-making.

label: Edmund Husserl
summary: Edmund Husserl (1859–1938) was a German philosopher widely regarded as the founder of phenomenology, the philosophical study of the structures of consciousness and experience as they are given from a first-person point of view. Central to his work is the notion of intentionality — the directedness of consciousness toward objects — which he developed in works such as Logical Investigations and Ideas. His phenomenological method influenced later philosophy, including existentialism and, more broadly, the philosophy of cognitive science.

label: Élie Metchnikoff
summary: Élie Metchnikoff (1845–1916) was a zoologist from the Russian Empire best known for his research in immunology, and he and Paul Ehrlich were jointly awarded the 1908 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in recognition of their work on immunity. Honoured as the "father of innate immunity", he was the first to discover the immune process of phagocytosis and the cell responsible for it in 1882, laying a foundation for the concept of cell-mediated immunity. His and Ehrlich's works are together regarded as the foundation of the science of immunology.

label: Emil Kraepelin
summary: Emil Kraepelin (1856–1926) was a German psychiatrist identified by Hans Eysenck's Encyclopedia of Psychology as partially responsible for laying the foundations of modern scientific psychiatry, psychopharmacology, and psychiatric genetics. He believed the chief origin of psychiatric disease to be a combination of biological process and genetic disorder, and his theories dominated psychiatry at the start of the 20th century, enjoying a revival at the century's end despite the intervening psychodynamic influence of Sigmund Freud. He has been described as a "scientific manager" who developed a large-scale, clinically oriented, epidemiological research programme.

label: Émile Durkheim
summary: Émile Durkheim (1858–1917) was a French sociologist widely regarded as one of the principal founders of sociology as an academic discipline. He argued that societies should be studied through "social facts" — ways of acting and thinking that are external to and coercive upon individuals — and applied this program in studies of the division of labor, suicide, and religion, set out in works such as The Rules of Sociological Method. His work also influenced anthropology, and he is commonly credited with helping to establish sociology's distinctive methods and subject matter.

label: Emmy Noether
summary: Emmy Noether (1882–1935) was a German mathematician widely regarded as a founder of modern abstract algebra, who developed theories of rings, fields, and algebras that reshaped the discipline. In her 1921 paper Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen she developed the theory of ideals in commutative rings into a widely applicable tool, and objects satisfying her ascending chain condition are called Noetherian in her honor. In physics, Noether's theorem explains the connection between symmetry and conservation laws, a result that has profoundly influenced the development of modern physics.

label: Ernst Chladni
summary: Ernst Chladni (1756–1827) was a German physicist and musician whose most important work, for which he is sometimes labeled the father of acoustics, included research on vibrating plates and the calculation of the speed of sound for different gases. He also undertook pioneering work in the study of meteorites and is regarded by some as the father of meteoritics. His experiments on the vibration of plates are foundational to the physical study of sound.

label: Ernst Haeckel
summary: Ernst Haeckel (1834–1919) was a German zoologist, naturalist, and philosopher who discovered, described, and named thousands of new species and coined many terms in biology, including ecology, phylum, phylogeny, and ontogeny. He promoted and popularised Charles Darwin's work in Germany and developed the disproven but influential recapitulation theory, summed up by the dictum "ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny". His illustrated Kunstformen der Natur went on to influence the Art Nouveau movement, though he also promoted scientific racism and Social Darwinism.

label: Eugenius Warming
summary: Eugenius Warming (1841–1924) was a Danish botanist and a pioneering figure in the development of ecology. In 1895 he published Plantesamfund, often regarded as the first textbook on plant ecology, and he taught an early university course in ecology. The ecologist Robert J. Goodland wrote that if one individual were to be singled out as the founder of ecology, Warming should gain precedence.

label: Ferdinand de Saussure
summary: Ferdinand de Saussure (1857–1913) was a Swiss linguist and philosopher widely regarded as a founder of modern structural linguistics and, together with Charles Sanders Peirce, as one of two major founders of semiotics (which he called semiology). His posthumously published Cours de linguistique générale set out the structural approach to language, distinguishing the sign's signifier and signified and treating language as a system of relations. His ideas reshaped 20th-century linguistics and the study of signs, and influenced structuralist thinkers such as Claude Lévi-Strauss.

label: Franz Boas
summary: Franz Boas (1858–1942) was a German-American anthropologist widely regarded as a founder of modern cultural anthropology, often called the "Father of American Anthropology." A leading proponent of cultural relativism and a prominent opponent of the scientific racism of his day, he argued that human behavior is shaped largely by culture acquired through social learning rather than by innate biological traits. Through his many influential students and works such as The Mind of Primitive Man, Boas profoundly shaped American anthropology and debates about race.

label: Franz Brentano
summary: Franz Brentano (1838–1917) was a German philosopher and psychologist whose 1874 book Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint, regarded as his major work, is credited with bringing the scholastic-era notion of intentionality — the idea that mental acts are directed at objects — back into modern philosophical discussion. He trained and served as a Catholic priest before withdrawing in 1873 over the church's newly declared dogma of papal infallibility, and in 1874 took a full professorship at the University of Vienna. He lost that position in 1880: Austro-Hungarian law barred former priests from marrying, and after he and Ida von Lieben wed abroad the authorities declined to reinstate him, so he taught on as an unsalaried Privatdozent until 1895. His Vienna students included Edmund Husserl, Sigmund Freud, Alexius Meinong, Carl Stumpf, and Kazimierz Twardowski. Husserl, who studied under Brentano before founding the phenomenological movement, carried the concept of intentionality forward along his own, distinct lines rather than co-originating it. Drawing heavily on Aristotle and later scholastic philosophy, Brentano is now often described as anticipating both the phenomenological and analytic traditions in twentieth-century philosophy.

label: Friedrich Nietzsche
summary: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German philosopher and philologist whose work addressed morality, religion, culture, and the nature of value, developing themes such as the critique of traditional morality, the "will to power," and perspectivism. Writing in works including Thus Spoke Zarathustra and Beyond Good and Evil, he became one of the most influential figures in modern thought. He is commonly cited as a major influence on existentialism, continental philosophy, and critical theory, and his reception drew on and reacted against earlier thinkers such as Arthur Schopenhauer.

label: Friedrich Waismann
summary: Friedrich Waismann (1896–1959) was an Austrian mathematician, physicist, and philosopher. He is best known for being a member of the Vienna Circle and one of the key theorists in logical positivism. His association with the Circle placed him among the central figures of that movement in early twentieth-century philosophy.

label: Georg Cantor
summary: Georg Cantor (1845–1918) was a mathematician widely regarded as the founder of set theory, which became a fundamental theory in mathematics. He established the importance of one-to-one correspondence between sets, defined infinite and well-ordered sets, and proved that the real numbers are more numerous than the natural numbers, developing a theory of transfinite cardinal and ordinal numbers. His work, controversial and resisted by contemporaries such as Henri Poincaré, was later defended by David Hilbert, who declared that no one should expel mathematicians from the paradise Cantor had created.

label: George Boole
summary: George Boole (1815–1864) was an English mathematician, philosopher, and logician widely regarded as a founder of modern mathematical logic, best known as the author of The Laws of Thought (1854), which contains Boolean algebra. He developed this algebra of logic, which laid the groundwork for the algebra of logic tradition and forms the foundation of digital circuit design and modern computer science. His ideas were expanded by scholars such as Charles Sanders Peirce, and later Claude Shannon employed Boolean algebra in the design of electrical switching systems, helping lay the foundations for the Information Age.

label: G. E. Moore
summary: G. E. Moore (1873–1958) was an English philosopher who, alongside Bertrand Russell, Ludwig Wittgenstein, and earlier Gottlob Frege, was an initiator of analytic philosophy. He and Russell began de-emphasising the idealism then prevalent among British philosophers and became known for advocating common-sense concepts and contributing to ethics, epistemology, and metaphysics. As Professor of Philosophy at the University of Cambridge he edited the journal Mind and was described by Ray Monk as "the most revered philosopher of his era".

label: George Lakoff
summary: George Lakoff (born 1941) is an American cognitive linguist and philosopher, best known for his thesis that people's lives are significantly influenced by the conceptual metaphors they use to explain complex phenomena. His conceptual metaphor thesis was introduced in his and Mark Johnson's 1980 book Metaphors We Live By and has found applications in a number of academic disciplines. He served as professor of linguistics at the University of California, Berkeley, from 1972 until his retirement in 2016.

label: George A. Miller
summary: George A. Miller (1920–2012) was an American psychologist who was one of the founders of cognitive psychology and, more broadly, of cognitive science, and he also contributed to the birth of psycholinguistics. He authored the paper "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two," observing an average limit of about seven items for human short-term memory capacity, and directed the development of the WordNet database. Rejecting the then-reigning behaviorism, he devised experimental techniques and mathematical methods to analyze mental processes, and is considered one of the great twentieth-century psychologists.

label: Georges Cuvier
summary: Georges Cuvier (1769–1832) was a French naturalist and zoologist sometimes referred to as the "founding father of paleontology," and was instrumental in establishing the fields of comparative anatomy and paleontology by comparing living animals with fossils. His work is considered the foundation of vertebrate paleontology, and he established extinction as a scientific fact at a time when it was widely regarded as controversial speculation. He was also the most influential proponent of catastrophism in early nineteenth-century geology.

label: Georgius Agricola
summary: Georgius Agricola (1494–1555) was a German Renaissance humanist scholar, mineralogist, and metallurgist who took a particular interest in the mining and refining of metals. For his groundbreaking work De Natura Fossilium, published in 1546, he is generally referred to as the father of mineralogy and the founder of geology as a scientific discipline. He is also well known for De re metallica libri XII, a comprehensive study of mining and metallurgy published one year after his death, which served as the standard reference work for two centuries.

label: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
summary: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) was a German polymath, mathematician, and philosopher who is credited, alongside Isaac Newton, with the creation of calculus, which he developed independently of Newton's work. His notation for calculus has been favored as the conventional and more exact expression of the subject and remains in use today; he is also credited with devising the modern binary number system that underlies digital computing. A leading rationalist philosopher whose vision of formal reasoning is cited as a distant precursor to computability theory, his work anticipated modern logic and still influences contemporary analytic philosophy.

label: Gottlob Frege
summary: Gottlob Frege (1848–1925) was a German logician, mathematician, and philosopher widely regarded as a founder of modern mathematical logic and analytic philosophy of language. In his Begriffsschrift (1879) he introduced a formal system of quantified logic that transformed the discipline, and he developed foundational analyses of concepts such as sense and reference. His work is commonly credited with helping to establish mathematical logic and the philosophy of language, and it influenced later work in linguistics.

label: Gregor Mendel
summary: Gregor Mendel (1822–1884) was an Austrian biologist and Augustinian friar widely regarded as the founder of the modern science of genetics. His pea plant experiments, conducted between 1856 and 1863, established many of the rules of heredity now known as the laws of Mendelian inheritance, published in 1866. The profound significance of his work went unrecognized until its rediscovery around 1900, when researchers independently verified his findings and ushered in the modern age of genetics.

label: Grove Karl Gilbert
summary: Grove Karl Gilbert (1843–1918), known in academic literature by the abbreviated name G. K. Gilbert, was an American geologist. His geological studies are associated with the development of the field of geomorphology.

label: Hans Hahn
summary: Hans Hahn (1879–1934) was an Austrian mathematician and philosopher who made contributions to functional analysis, topology, set theory, the calculus of variations, real analysis, and order theory. In philosophy he was among the main logical positivists of the Vienna Circle. His association with the Circle placed him among the central figures of that early twentieth-century movement.

label: Henri Poincaré
summary: Henri Poincaré (1854–1912) was a French mathematician, theoretical physicist, and philosopher of science widely regarded as the creator of the field of algebraic topology. In his research on the three-body problem he became the first person to discover a chaotic deterministic system, laying foundations of modern chaos theory and the study of dynamical systems, and he later formulated the Poincaré conjecture. A skeptic of Cantorian set theory, he was among the contemporaries who resisted Cantor's transfinite mathematics.

label: Herbert Feigl
summary: Herbert Feigl (1902–1988) was an Austrian-American philosopher and an early member of the Vienna Circle. He coined the term "nomological danglers". His membership placed him among the figures associated with the Circle's philosophical movement.

label: Herbert A. Simon
summary: Herbert A. Simon (1916–2001) was an American polymath whose contributions spanned computer science, economics, and cognitive psychology; he is best known for the concepts of bounded rationality and satisficing in decision-making. Together with Allen Newell, he built some of the earliest artificial intelligence programs, including the Logic Theory Machine (1956) and the General Problem Solver (1957); that work is often cited as foundational to artificial intelligence and to neighboring fields such as operations research, management science, and cognitive science. Simon and Newell shared the 1975 ACM Turing Award, and in 1978 Simon alone received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his research into decision-making within economic organizations.

label: Isaac Newton
summary: Isaac Newton (1643–1727) was an English mathematician and physicist who was a key figure in the Scientific Revolution and is regarded as one of two independent inventors of infinitesimal calculus, which he developed independently of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. In his Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687) he formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation, achieving the first great unification in physics and establishing classical mechanics. He also made seminal contributions to optics, collected in his 1704 book Opticks, and his work is considered among the most influential in bringing forth modern science.

label: Ivan Sutherland
summary: Ivan Sutherland (born 1938) is an American computer scientist widely regarded as a pioneer of computer graphics. He received the 1988 ACM Turing Award for the invention of the Sketchpad, an early predecessor to the graphical user interface, and his contributions to computer graphics. He is a member of the National Academy of Engineering and the National Academy of Sciences, and in 2012 was awarded the Kyoto Prize in Advanced Technology for "pioneering achievements in the development of computer graphics and interactive interfaces".

label: James Hutton
summary: James Hutton (1726–1797) was a Scottish geologist, naturalist, and physician often referred to as the "Father of Modern Geology," who played a key role in establishing geology as a modern science. He advanced the idea that the physical world's remote history can be inferred from evidence in present-day rocks and was one of the earliest proponents of what later became known as uniformitarianism. Though similar reflections appeared in the work of contemporaries such as Buffon, it is chiefly Hutton's pioneering work that established the field.

label: Jan Tinbergen
summary: Jan Tinbergen (1903–1994) was a Dutch economist who was awarded the first Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1969, which he shared with Ragnar Frisch for developing and applying dynamic models for the analysis of economic processes. He is widely considered one of the most influential economists of the 20th century and one of the founding fathers of econometrics. His contributions include the development of the first macroeconometric models and the solution of the identification problem.

label: Jean Piaget
summary: Jean Piaget (1896–1980) was a Swiss psychologist widely regarded as a founder of developmental psychology, known for his work on child development. His theory of cognitive development and his epistemological view are together called genetic epistemology, and his account of how children construct knowledge established development as a major sub-discipline in psychology. Described as the great pioneer of the constructivist theory of knowing, his ideas were widely popularized in the 1960s, and by the end of the 20th century he was second only to B. F. Skinner as the most-cited psychologist.

label: John Graunt
summary: John Graunt (1620–1674) has been regarded as the founder of demography. He was one of the first demographers, and perhaps the first epidemiologist, though by profession he was a haberdasher. His early analysis of mortality records is considered foundational to the statistical study of populations.

label: John McCarthy
summary: John McCarthy (1927–2011) was an American computer scientist and cognitive scientist who was one of the founders of the discipline of artificial intelligence. He co-authored the proposal for the Dartmouth workshop that coined the term "artificial intelligence," led the development of the Lisp programming language family, and created garbage collection. He spent most of his career at Stanford University and received the 1971 Turing Award for his contributions to AI.

label: John Milne
summary: John Milne (1850–1913) was a British geologist and mining engineer who worked on a horizontal seismograph. His instrument work is associated with the development of the study of earthquakes.

label: John Nash
summary: John Nash (1928–2015) was an American mathematician who made fundamental contributions to game theory, real algebraic geometry, differential geometry, and partial differential equations. As a graduate student at Princeton he introduced concepts including the Nash equilibrium, now considered central to game theory and its applications across the sciences, and extended equilibrium analysis to non-cooperative games. For these contributions he shared the 1994 Nobel Prize in Economics with fellow game theorists John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten, and in 2015 received the Abel Prize for his work on partial differential equations.

label: John Snow
summary: John Snow (1813–1858) was an English physician and a leader in the development of anaesthesia and medical hygiene. He is considered one of the founders of modern epidemiology, in part because of his work in tracing the source of a cholera outbreak in London's Soho to a particular public water pump. His findings inspired fundamental changes in the water and waste systems of London and a significant improvement in general public health.

label: John Tooby
summary: John Tooby (1952–2023) was an American anthropologist who, together with his psychologist wife Leda Cosmides, pioneered the field of evolutionary psychology. His collaborative work with Cosmides is credited with shaping that field's foundations.

label: John von Neumann
summary: John von Neumann (1903–1957) was a Hungarian and American mathematician, physicist, and computer scientist who, with Oskar Morgenstern in Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, was a co-founder of game theory. His work spanned mathematics, physics, economics, computing, and statistics, and he helped establish the mathematical framework of quantum physics and functional analysis. His formalization of a stored-program design influenced the architecture of modern computer systems.

label: Karl Ernst von Baer
summary: Karl Ernst von Baer (1792–1876) was a Baltic German scientist and explorer—naturalist, biologist, geologist, and geographer—who is widely considered a founding father of embryology, the study of animal development. He conducted pioneering work on the development of the embryo, and is regarded as a foundational figure for developmental biology. He was also a member of the Russian Academy of Sciences and a co-founder of the Russian Geographical Society.

label: Karl Marx
summary: Karl Marx (1818–1883) was a German philosopher, economist, and social theorist whose analysis of capitalism, class, and history has been widely influential across the social sciences, including sociology. In works such as Capital (Das Kapital), he analyzed the workings of capitalist production, value, and class relations, developing a materialist conception of history. His ideas are closely associated with the concept of false consciousness and gave rise to a broad tradition of Marxist thought in economics, politics, sociology, and philosophy.

label: Karl Pearson
summary: Karl Pearson (1857–1936) was an English biostatistician and mathematician widely credited with establishing the discipline of mathematical statistics. He founded the world's first university statistics department at University College London in 1911 and contributed significantly to the field of biometrics. A protégé and biographer of Francis Galton, his statistical methods influenced the social sciences, though he was also a proponent of eugenics and Social Darwinism.

label: Kenneth Arrow
summary: Kenneth Arrow (1921–2017) was an American economist, mathematician, and political theorist widely regarded as a founder of modern social choice theory, and a major figure in postwar neoclassical economic theory. His contributions to social choice theory, notably his impossibility theorem, together with his work on general equilibrium analysis, are among his most significant achievements. He received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1972 along with John Hicks, and his work on endogenous growth theory and the economics of information was also foundational.

label: Kurt Gödel
summary: Kurt Gödel (1906–1978) was a logician, mathematician, and philosopher regarded as one of the most significant logicians in history. He is best known for his incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, which address the limitations of formal axiomatic systems; to prove them he developed the technique now known as Gödel numbering, which codes formal expressions as natural numbers. His discoveries profoundly influenced scientific and philosophical thinking in the 20th century and were associated with the foundational research of figures such as Bertrand Russell and David Hilbert.

label: Kurt Lewin
summary: Kurt Lewin (1890–1947) was a German-American psychologist regarded as one of the modern pioneers of social, organizational, and applied psychology in the United States. He is often recognized as the "founder of social psychology" and was among the first to study group dynamics and organizational development. A 2002 survey ranked him as the 18th-most cited psychologist of the 20th century.

label: Leda Cosmides
summary: Leda Cosmides (born 1957) is an American psychologist who, together with anthropologist John Tooby, pioneered the field of evolutionary psychology. Her work with Tooby is widely credited with establishing evolutionary psychology as a research program. She is recognized as a co-founder of the field.

label: Louis Pasteur
summary: Louis Pasteur (1822–1895) was a French chemist, pharmacist, and microbiologist renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization. He is regarded as one of the founders of modern bacteriology and has been honored as the "father of microbiology" (together with Robert Koch). His work disproving spontaneous generation and supporting the germ theory of disease laid foundations for hygiene, public health, and much of modern medicine.

label: Luciano Floridi
summary: Luciano Floridi (born 1964) is an Italian and British philosopher best known for his work in the philosophy of information and information ethics. He is John K. Castle Professor in the Practice of Cognitive Science and Founding Director of the Digital Ethics Center at Yale University, and was the founder and director of the interdepartmental research group on the philosophy of information at the University of Oxford. He has received many awards, including the Knight of the Grand Cross of the Order of Merit, and according to Scopus was the most cited living philosopher in the world in 2020.

label: Ludwig Wittgenstein
summary: Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951) was an Austro-British philosopher who worked in logic, philosophy of mathematics, philosophy of mind, and philosophy of language, and is regarded as a foundational figure in the philosophy of language. His early work, the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921), examined the logical relationship between propositions and the world and strongly influenced logical positivism. His later thought, articulated in the posthumous Philosophical Investigations, argued instead that the meaning of words is best understood as their use within a language game.

label: Martin Hellman
summary: Martin Hellman (born 1945) is an American cryptologist and mathematician, best known for his invention of public-key cryptography in cooperation with Whitfield Diffie and Ralph Merkle. He was elected a member of the National Academy of Engineering in 2002 for contributions to the theory and practice of cryptography. In 2015, he and Whitfield Diffie won the ACM Turing Award.

label: Martin Seligman
summary: Martin Seligman (born 1942) is an American psychologist widely regarded as a strong promoter of positive psychology within the scientific community. He is the Zellerbach Family Professor of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania and director of the university's Positive Psychology Center, and his theory of learned helplessness is well known among scientific and clinical psychologists. He was elected president of the American Psychological Association for 1998, and a 2002 Review of General Psychology survey ranked him as the 31st most cited psychologist of the 20th century.

label: Marvin Minsky
summary: Marvin Minsky (1927–2016) was an American mathematician who conducted research in the cognitive and computer science aspects of artificial intelligence (AI). He joined MIT in 1958, where he co-founded the institution's AI laboratory, and—alongside computer scientist John McCarthy and others—has been called one of the "fathers of AI." He received many honors for his work, including the ACM Turing Award in 1969.

label: Mathieu Orfila
summary: Mathieu Orfila (1787–1853) was a Spanish-born French toxicologist and chemist, regarded as the father of modern toxicology. His work established the scientific study of poisons and their effects, and he is credited as a founding figure of toxicology as a discipline.

label: Matthew Fontaine Maury
summary: Matthew Fontaine Maury (1806–1873) was an American oceanographer and naval officer, nicknamed the "Pathfinder of the Seas" and considered a founder of modern oceanography. His book The Physical Geography of the Sea (1855) was the first comprehensive work on oceanography to be published. His uniform system of recording oceanographic data was adopted by navies and merchant marines worldwide.

label: Matthias Jakob Schleiden
summary: Matthias Jakob Schleiden (1804–1881) was a German botanist and a co-founder of cell theory, along with Theodor Schwann and Rudolf Virchow. His formulation of cell theory—that plants are composed of cells—is foundational to cell biology.

label: Max Weber
summary: Max Weber (1864–1920) was a German sociologist, historian, and political economist widely regarded as one of the founders of modern sociology. He is known for analyses of rationalization, authority, and bureaucracy, for his interpretive (verstehen) approach to social action, and for The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, which argued for a connection between certain religious ideas and the development of capitalism. His account of social and economic development is often contrasted with that of Karl Marx.

label: Michael Gazzaniga
summary: Michael Gazzaniga (born 1939) is an American cognitive neuroscientist and professor emeritus of psychology at the University of California, Santa Barbara. He is widely recognized as a founding figure in cognitive neuroscience. He is the founder and retired director of the SAGE Center for the Study of the Mind at UCSB, which he directed from 2006 to 2023.

label: Moritz Schlick
summary: Moritz Schlick (1882–1936) was a German philosopher and physicist described as the founding father of logical positivism and the Vienna Circle. He led the Vienna Circle until he was murdered by a former student in 1936.

label: Noam Chomsky
summary: Noam Chomsky is an American linguist and cognitive scientist widely credited with founding generative grammar, an approach that treats a language's grammar as a finite system of explicit rules generating its grammatical sentences and as a representation of speakers' tacit linguistic knowledge. His work introduced the influential hypothesis of an innate universal grammar and helped shift linguistics and cognitive science toward the study of the mind, contributing to the mid-twentieth-century "cognitive revolution." He is also widely known as a public intellectual.

label: Norbert Wiener
summary: Norbert Wiener (1894–1964) was an American mathematician, computer scientist, and philosopher widely regarded as the originator of cybernetics, the science of communication and control in living things and machines. A professor of mathematics at MIT, he did early work on stochastic and mathematical noise processes relevant to communication and control systems. His ideas about feedback and intelligent behavior influenced figures including John von Neumann and Claude Shannon and helped shape cognitive psychology and early artificial intelligence.

label: Oskar Morgenstern
summary: Oskar Morgenstern (1902–1977) was a German-born economist who, in collaboration with mathematician John von Neumann, is credited with founding the field of game theory and its application to the social sciences and strategic decision-making. He also made significant contributions to decision theory, including the von Neumann–Morgenstern utility theorem.

label: Oswald Schmiedeberg
summary: Oswald Schmiedeberg (1838–1921) was a Baltic German pharmacologist who became the first professor of pharmacology at the University of Strasbourg, where he remained for 46 years. Having trained most of the European professors of his era, he is regarded as a founding figure of modern pharmacology and was a major factor in the success of the German pharmaceutical industry.

label: Otto Neurath
summary: Otto Neurath (1882–1945) was an Austrian-born philosopher of science, sociologist, and political economist, and one of the leading figures of the Vienna Circle. A proponent of logical positivism, he was also known for inventing the ISOTYPE method of pictorial statistics and for innovations in museum practice. He fled his native country in 1934.

label: Paul Ehrlich
summary: Paul Ehrlich (1854–1915) was a German physician and scientist who worked in the fields of hematology, immunology, and antimicrobial chemotherapy, and has been called the "father of immunology." He shared the 1908 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Élie Metchnikoff for their work on immunity, and his laboratory discovered the first effective treatment for syphilis, initiating the concept of chemotherapy.

label: Philipp Frank
summary: Philipp Frank (1884–1966) was an Austrian-American physicist, mathematician, and philosopher of the early-to-mid 20th century. He was a logical positivist and a member of the Vienna Circle, and was influenced by Ernst Mach.

label: Philippe Pinel
summary: Philippe Pinel (1745–1826) was a French physician and precursor of psychiatry who has been described by some as "the father of modern psychiatry." He was instrumental in the development of a more humane approach to the care of psychiatric patients—later known as moral therapy—and worked to abolish the shackling of mental patients. He also made notable contributions to the classification of mental disorders.

label: Ragnar Frisch
summary: Ragnar Frisch (1895–1973) was an influential Norwegian economist and econometrician, and one of the major contributors to establishing economics as a quantitative, statistically informed science. He coined the term econometrics in 1926 and was a founder of the Econometric Society in 1930. His later work on business-cycle modeling, together with Jan Tinbergen, won the first Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1969.

label: René Just Haüy
summary: René Just Haüy (1743–1822) was a French priest and mineralogist, commonly styled the Abbé Haüy. For his innovative work on crystal structure and his four-volume Traité de Minéralogie (1801), he is often referred to as the "Father of Modern Crystallography." During the French Revolution he also helped to establish the metric system.

label: Richard Dedekind
summary: Richard Dedekind (1831–1916) was a German mathematician who made important contributions to number theory, abstract algebra, and the axiomatic foundations of arithmetic. He is considered a pioneer in the development of modern set theory and of the philosophy of mathematics known as logicism. His best-known contribution is the definition of real numbers through the notion of the Dedekind cut.

label: Richard Thaler
summary: Richard Thaler (born 1945) is an American economist and a theorist in behavioral economics, serving as the Charles R. Walgreen Distinguished Service Professor of Behavioral Science and Economics at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business. In 2017 he was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his contributions to behavioral economics. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences stated that his contributions have been instrumental in creating the new and rapidly expanding field of behavioral economics.

label: Robert Koch
summary: Robert Koch (1843–1910) was a German physician and microbiologist who won the 1905 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on tuberculosis. As the discoverer of the causative agents of tuberculosis, cholera, and anthrax, he is regarded as one of the main founders of modern bacteriology and is popularly nicknamed the father of microbiology (with Louis Pasteur). His work provided direct proof for the germ theory of disease and formalized Koch's postulates.

label: Roman Jakobson
summary: Roman Jakobson (1896–1982) was a Russian linguist and literary theorist, a pioneer of structural linguistics who, with Nikolai Trubetzkoy, developed new techniques for analyzing linguistic sound systems, in effect founding the modern discipline of phonology. His celebrated theory of distinctive features articulated underlying linguistic universals and decisively influenced the early thinking of Noam Chomsky. Through his influence on Claude Lévi-Strauss and others, and drawing on C. S. Peirce's semiotics, Jakobson helped extend structural analysis to disciplines beyond linguistics.

label: Ronald Fisher
summary: Ronald Fisher (1890–1962) was a British polymath, active as a mathematician, statistician, biologist, and geneticist, widely regarded as a founder of modern mathematical statistics. Working at the Rothamsted Experimental Station, he developed the analysis of variance (ANOVA), the method of maximum likelihood, and the principles of the design of experiments, and he also helped found population genetics. His statistical methods, developed partly in a well-known rivalry with Karl Pearson, went on to influence fields such as epidemiology.

label: Ronald Langacker
summary: Ronald Langacker (born 1942) is an American linguist and professor emeritus at the University of California, San Diego, best known as one of the founders of the cognitive linguistics movement and the creator of cognitive grammar. He has also made significant contributions to the comparative study of Uto-Aztecan languages. He has published several articles on historical Uto-Aztecan linguistics and edited collections of grammar sketches of under-described Uto-Aztecan languages.

label: Rudolf Carnap
summary: Rudolf Carnap (1891–1970) was a German philosopher and logician who was active in Europe before 1935 and in the United States thereafter. He was a major member of the Vienna Circle and an advocate of logical positivism.

label: Samuel Eilenberg
summary: Samuel Eilenberg (1913–1998) was a Polish-American mathematician who co-founded category theory—together with Saunders Mac Lane—as well as homological algebra. Category theory grew from this collaborative work into a foundational area of modern mathematics.

label: Saunders Mac Lane
summary: Saunders Mac Lane (1909–2005) was an American mathematician who co-founded category theory together with Samuel Eilenberg. Their collaborative work established category theory as a foundational framework in modern mathematics.

label: Sigmund Freud
summary: Sigmund Freud (1856–1939) was an Austrian neurologist who founded psychoanalysis, a theory of the mind and a method for treating psychological disorders centered on the idea that unconscious mental processes shape thought and behavior. He developed influential concepts including the unconscious, repression, and the interpretation of dreams, and set them out in works such as The Interpretation of Dreams (1899/1900). His ideas were widely influential across psychology, psychiatry, and the humanities, including literary studies, while also drawing sustained scientific and philosophical criticism.

label: Stephen Cook
summary: Stephen Cook (born 1939) is an American-Canadian computer scientist and mathematician widely considered one of the forefathers of computational complexity theory. He has made significant contributions to the fields of complexity theory and proof complexity, and is a university professor emeritus at the University of Toronto. He won the 1982 ACM Turing Award.

label: Theodor Schwann
summary: Theodor Schwann (1810–1882) was a German physician and physiologist whose most significant contribution to biology is considered to be the extension of cell theory to animals—foundational work for cell biology. His other contributions include the discovery of Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system, the discovery of pepsin, and the coining of the term "metabolism."

label: Ulric Neisser
summary: Ulric Neisser (1928–2012) was a German-American psychologist and Cornell University professor who has been referred to as the "father of cognitive psychology." In 1967 he published Cognitive Psychology, which brought him instant recognition in the field and was considered an attack on behaviorist paradigms. He researched perception and memory, arguing that memory is largely reconstructed rather than a snapshot of the moment.

label: Victor Moritz Goldschmidt
summary: Victor Moritz Goldschmidt (1888–1947) was a Norwegian-Jewish mineralogist considered—together with Vladimir Vernadsky—to be the founder of modern geochemistry and crystal chemistry. He is also known as the developer of the Goldschmidt Classification of elements.

label: Vint Cerf
summary: Vint Cerf (born 1943) is an American Internet pioneer recognized as one of "the fathers of the Internet", sharing this title with TCP/IP co-developer Robert Kahn. He is widely credited, alongside Kahn, with the co-development of the TCP/IP protocols underlying the Internet. He has received honorary degrees and awards including the National Medal of Technology, the Turing Award, the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and membership in the National Academy of Engineering.

label: Vladimir Vernadsky
summary: Vladimir Vernadsky (1863–1945) was a Russian, Ukrainian, and Soviet mineralogist and geochemist who is considered one of the founders of geochemistry, biogeochemistry, and radiogeology. He was also a founder and the first president of the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences. He is most noted for his 1926 book The Biosphere, in which he hypothesized that life is a geological force that shapes the earth.

label: Whitfield Diffie
summary: Whitfield Diffie (born 1944) is an American cryptographer and mathematician, and one of the pioneers of public-key cryptography along with Martin Hellman and Ralph Merkle. Diffie and Hellman's 1976 paper New Directions in Cryptography introduced a radically new method of distributing cryptographic keys, and their technique became known as Diffie-Hellman key exchange. He later served as Vice President for Information Security and Cryptography at ICANN and as a visiting scholar at Stanford University's Center for International Security and Cooperation.

label: Wilhelm Wundt
summary: Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920) was a German physiologist and philosopher widely regarded as the "father of experimental psychology" and one of the fathers of modern psychology, being the first person to call himself a psychologist. In 1879, at the University of Leipzig, he founded the first formal laboratory for psychological research, an event that marked psychology as an independent field of study distinct from philosophy and biology. He also established the first academic journal for psychological research, Philosophische Studien, to publish his institute's work.

label: William Labov
summary: William Labov (1927–2024) was an American linguist widely regarded as the founder of the discipline of variationist sociolinguistics. He has been described as an enormously original and influential figure who created much of the methodology of sociolinguistics, and as one of the most influential linguists of the 20th and 21st centuries. He was a professor in the linguistics department of the University of Pennsylvania.

label: William Morris Davis
summary: William Morris Davis (1850–1934) was an American geographer, geologist, geomorphologist, and meteorologist, often called the "father of American geography." He studied geology and geography at Harvard and later taught there, and his legacy lives on in geomorphology, the study of landforms. He is regarded as a founding figure of geomorphology as a field.

label: Accelerator Physics
summary: Accelerator physics concerns the production, behavior, and use of beams of charged particles and the instruments that generate them. The American Physical Society's Division of Physics of Beams gives its objective as "the advancement and diffusion of knowledge regarding the nature and behavior of beams and the instruments for their production and use." The principal instruments of the field, particle accelerators, are described by Encyclopaedia Britannica as "any device that produces a beam of fast-moving, electrically charged atomic or subatomic particles," used "in fundamental research on the structure of nuclei, the nature of nuclear forces, and the properties of nuclei not found in nature." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society the field appears as the discipline "Accelerators & Beams."

label: Acoustics
summary: Acoustics is the science of sound—its production, control, transmission, reception, and effects. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "science concerned with the production, control, transmission, reception, and effects of sound," noting that it began "with its origins in the study of mechanical vibrations and the radiation of these vibrations through mechanical waves." Within the Universal Decimal Classification the field is grouped under UDC 534 'Vibrations. Waves. Acoustics,' reflecting its grounding in vibration and wave phenomena.

label: Aesthetics
summary: Aesthetics is the branch of philosophy concerned with the nature of beauty, art, and aesthetic experience, as well as the principles governing judgments of taste. Central questions include what makes something beautiful or sublime, how artworks convey meaning, and whether aesthetic judgments are objective or subjective. The field overlaps substantially with the philosophy of art.

label: Affective Neuroscience
summary: Affective neuroscience is the study of how the brain processes emotions. This field combines neuroscience with the psychological study of personality, emotion, and mood. The basis of emotions and what emotions are remains an issue of debate within the field of affective neuroscience.

label: African Philosophy
summary: African philosophy encompasses the philosophical traditions, arguments, and concepts that have developed in Africa or among people of African descent, including oral traditions, indigenous thought systems, and academic philosophical work. Recognized currents include ethnophilosophy (the study of collective African worldviews), sage philosophy, African communitarian ethics (Ubuntu), and Africana philosophy addressing the experiences of the African diaspora. The field raises foundational questions about the definition of philosophy and the relationship between oral and written traditions.

label: Algebra
summary: Algebra is the branch of mathematics that studies algebraic structures — sets equipped with one or more binary operations satisfying prescribed axioms — including groups, rings, fields, and modules. Group theory, whose objects are sets with a single associative binary operation closed under inverses, is historically one of the first examples of an abstract algebraic system and served as a model for the restructuring of other mathematical disciplines. Commutative algebra, homological algebra, and the theory of non-associative algebras are among the principal sub-disciplines, with connections to number theory, algebraic geometry, and topology.

label: Algebraic Geometry
summary: Algebraic geometry is the branch of mathematics dealing with geometric objects defined by polynomial equations — classically algebraic curves and varieties — and their properties studied through the interplay of algebra, topology, and complex analysis. The field extends from the study of algebraic curves, classified by genus, to higher-dimensional varieties and, in its modern formulation, to schemes, the framework introduced to give a unified treatment of varieties over arbitrary fields. Arithmetic geometry, which applies the methods of algebraic geometry to the study of integer solutions of polynomial equations, is a major area with connections to number theory.

label: Algebraic Topology
summary: Algebraic topology is the branch of mathematics that studies topological spaces by associating algebraic invariants to them, with the aim of classifying spaces up to continuous deformation. Its primary tools include homology groups, which were introduced to measure topological features of spaces and originated in Henri Poincaré's 1895 work on polyhedra; homotopy groups, which classify continuous mappings; and cohomology rings, which carry additional algebraic structure dual to homology. The field also encompasses the study of fibre bundles, characteristic classes, and K-theory.

label: Algorithms and Data Structures
summary: Algorithms and data structures is the area of computer science concerned with the design and analysis of step-by-step computational procedures and the methods of organizing data on which they operate. The Encyclopedia of Mathematics defines an algorithm as "detailed instructions defining a computational process" that begins with an arbitrary input and proceeds by "consecutive conversion of constructive objects by discrete 'steps'," producing a result "fully determined by the input"; it also notes that the process "may also terminate without a result being obtained…or may not terminate at all." The word derives from the Latin transliteration of the name of the 9th-century mathematician al-Khwarizmi, and the modern theory of algorithms rests on twentieth-century formalizations by Turing, Post, Markov, and Kolmogorov together with the Church–Turing thesis.

label: Analytic Philosophy
summary: Analytic philosophy is a tradition in philosophy that emphasizes clarity of argument, logical rigor, and engagement with formal methods, and that developed primarily in the English-speaking world during the twentieth century. It emerged in the early twentieth century through the work of figures including Gottlob Frege, Bertrand Russell, G. E. Moore, and later Ludwig Wittgenstein, and has since become the dominant approach in Anglophone academic philosophy. Core areas include philosophy of language, philosophy of mind, logic, and formal epistemology.

label: Analytical Chemistry
summary: Analytical chemistry is the subfield of chemistry concerned with determining the composition of matter and the identity, quantity, and structure of its components. The Encyclopaedia Britannica, treating the subject under chemical analysis, describes it as the "determination of the physical properties or chemical composition of samples of matter," noting that "a large body of systematic procedures intended for these purposes has been continuously evolving in close association with the development of other branches of the physical sciences." The disciplinary community frames the field around measurement science: the journal Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry states that its scope covers "fundamental and applied topics of analytical and bioanalytical measurement science" and "ranges from novel measurement platforms and their characterization to multidisciplinary approaches." The subfield develops and applies methods of qualitative and quantitative analysis, instrumentation, and separation and detection techniques used throughout the natural sciences.

label: Anatomy
summary: Anatomy is the branch of morphology concerned with the study of the internal and external structure of organisms and their parts. A branch of natural science dealing with the structural organization of living things, it is among the oldest sciences. As a basic biomedical science it is cross-listed into medicine.

label: Ancient History
summary: Ancient history is the branch of historical study concerned with the period from the beginning of writing and recorded human history through late antiquity. As a time span it runs roughly across the period 3000 BC – AD 500 and covers all continents inhabited by humans during that era, ending with the expansion of Islam in late antiquity.

label: Ancient Philosophy
summary: Ancient philosophy refers to the philosophical traditions that developed in the ancient Mediterranean world, principally in Greece and Rome, from roughly the 6th century BCE through the late antique period. It includes pre-Socratic cosmology, the Platonic and Aristotelian schools, Hellenistic movements such as Stoicism and Epicureanism, and Neoplatonism. These traditions addressed questions in metaphysics, ethics, logic, and natural philosophy that continue to inform later Western philosophy.

label: Applied Linguistics
summary: Applied linguistics is an interdisciplinary field which identifies, investigates, and offers solutions to language-related real-life problems. Academic fields related to it include education, psychology, communication research, information science, natural language processing, anthropology, and sociology.

label: Applied Mathematics
summary: Applied mathematics is the branch of mathematics concerned with the development and use of mathematical methods to formulate and solve problems arising in the natural sciences, engineering, economics, and other disciplines outside pure mathematics. Its core areas include differential equations, mathematical modelling, numerical analysis, optimisation, probability and statistics, and mathematical physics. Applied mathematics is distinguished from pure mathematics by its orientation toward real-world problem-solving, though the boundary between the two is not sharp and many areas of applied mathematics have generated substantial pure theory.

label: Applied Statistics
summary: Applied statistics is the application-facing branch of statistics concerned with using statistical methods to analyze data arising in scientific, industrial, governmental, and social contexts. Its toolkit spans regression and correlation analysis, multivariate methods, experimental design, and survival analysis, and the field spans 'an enormous range from direct subject-matter collaborations to pure mathematical theory' as characterized by the Institute of Mathematical Statistics. Applied statistics draws on the theoretical apparatus of mathematical statistics and deploys it across domains such as healthcare, biology, engineering, education, and economics.

label: Art History
summary: Art history is an academic discipline devoted to the study of artistic production and visual culture throughout human history. Art historians apply a historical method or a philosophical framework—such as historical materialism or critical theory—to analyze artworks, studying art's impact on societies and cultures, the relationship between art and politics, and how styles and formal characteristics have changed over time. The discipline is distinguished from art criticism, which establishes relative artistic value, and from aesthetics, a branch of philosophy. The College Art Association, founded in 1911, "Promotes excellence in scholarship and teaching in the history and criticism of the visual arts." In the Library of Congress Classification, the history of the visual arts occupies the range N5300–N7418.

label: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Artificial intelligence is, in Britannica's definition, "the ability of a digital computer or computer-controlled robot to perform tasks commonly associated with intelligent beings," and the term denotes developing systems with intellectual processes characteristic of humans, including reasoning, generalization, and learning from experience. Britannica frames its core abilities as learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, and language use, and contrasts rote learning (memorization) with generalization (applying past experience to new situations). Digital computers have been programmed since the 1940s to carry out increasingly complex tasks, and Britannica notes that while some systems match human expert performance on specific tasks, no current program achieves full human flexibility across broader domains.

label: Astrophysics
summary: Astrophysics is the branch of astronomy that studies the physical properties, composition, and structure of celestial objects and of the universe as a whole, applying the laws of physics to understand cosmic phenomena. The Encyclopaedia Britannica characterizes it as the "branch of astronomy concerned primarily with the properties and structure of cosmic objects, including the universe as a whole." Its identity as a distinct division within astronomy is reflected in standard bibliographic classification: the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QB460-QB466 to "Astrophysics (General)" within the astronomy subclass QB. The field connects observational astronomy with theoretical physics, treating objects such as stars, galaxies, and interstellar matter as physical systems whose behavior can be modeled through the same principles that govern matter and energy on Earth.

label: Atmospheric Science
summary: Atmospheric science is the study of the structure, composition, and dynamics of Earth's atmosphere. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as an "interdisciplinary field of study that combines the components of physics and chemistry that focus on the structure and dynamics of Earth's atmosphere." As an umbrella discipline, it encompasses several traditional areas; Britannica notes that "the atmospheric sciences are traditionally divided into three topical areas—meteorology (the study and forecasting of weather), climatology (the study of long-term atmospheric patterns and their influences), and aeronomy (the study of the physics and chemistry of the upper atmosphere)." The field draws on mathematical and computational tools to describe physical and chemical processes spanning timescales from hourly weather changes to long-term climate, treating meteorology and climatology as branches within its scope rather than as separate disciplines.

label: Atomic, Molecular and Optical Physics
summary: Atomic, molecular and optical (AMO) physics concerns the structure of atoms and simple molecules and their interactions with electrons and with light. The American Physical Society's Division of Atomic, Molecular and Optical Physics (DAMOP) describes its "central focus" as "fundamental research on atoms, simple molecules, electrons and light, and their interactions," noting that it works "through the development of methods for the control and manipulation of atoms, molecules, charged particles and light, through precision measurements and calculations of their properties, and through the invention of new ways to generate light with specific properties." The atomic component is treated by Encyclopaedia Britannica as "the scientific study of the structure of the atom, its energy states, and its interactions with other particles and with electric and magnetic fields." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society the field appears as the discipline "Atomic, Molecular & Optical."

label: Automotive Engineering
summary: Automotive engineering, along with aerospace engineering and naval architecture, is a branch of vehicle engineering, incorporating elements of mechanical, electrical, electronic, software, and safety engineering as applied to the design, manufacture and operation of motorcycles, automobiles, and trucks and their respective engineering subsystems. The field is research-intensive and applies mathematical models to design, develop, fabricate, and test vehicles or vehicle components from concept to production. The Library of Congress Classification places motor vehicles in range TL1-TL483, captioned "Motor vehicles." The discipline's leading professional body, SAE International, was formerly the Society of Automotive Engineers and "adopted its current name in 2006 to reflect both its international membership and the increased scope of its activities beyond automotive engineering."

label: Axiology
summary: Axiology, also called value theory, is the philosophical study of value and goodness, primarily concerned with classifying what things are good and with theoretical questions about the nature of value. A central distinction is between intrinsic value (what is good in itself) and instrumental value (what is good as a means); broadly construed, value theory encompasses questions of value across moral, political, and aesthetic philosophy.

label: Bayesian Statistics
summary: Bayesian statistics is a paradigm of statistical inference in which unknown parameters are treated as random variables and uncertainty about them is expressed and updated via probability distributions. The framework proceeds by combining a prior distribution encoding existing knowledge with a likelihood derived from observed data to yield a posterior distribution, following Bayes's theorem. The paradigm has its own active research community and has proven especially effective for problems where frequentist approximations are difficult, though it remains philosophically contested because the choice of prior introduces an element of subjectivity.

label: Behavioral economics
summary: Behavioral economics is a subfield of economics that incorporates insights from psychology into the analysis of economic decision-making, studying how cognitive limitations, biases, and social and emotional factors lead people to depart systematically from the predictions of standard rational-choice models. It draws heavily on the work of Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky on judgment under uncertainty and prospect theory, and on later contributions to topics such as bounded rationality, framing effects, and self-control. The field applies these findings to areas including finance, public policy, and consumer behavior, and is closely related to behavioral finance.

label: Behavioral Neuroscience
summary: Behavioral neuroscience, also known as biological psychology, biopsychology, or psychobiology, is part of the broad, interdisciplinary field of neuroscience, with its primary focus being on the biological and neural substrates underlying human experiences and behaviors. Derived from an earlier field known as physiological psychology, it applies the principles of biology to study the physiological, genetic, and developmental mechanisms of behavior in humans and other animals.

label: Biblical Studies
summary: Biblical studies is the academic application of a set of diverse disciplines to the study of the Bible, examining its texts through historical and analytical methods rather than devotional ones. For its theory and methods the field draws on disciplines ranging from ancient history, historical criticism, philology, theology, textual criticism, and others.

label: Bibliometrics
summary: Bibliometrics is the application of statistical and quantitative methods to the study of the production, communication, and use of scientific and scholarly publications. The international journal Scientometrics describes its scope as "original research on all quantitative aspects of the production, communication, and use of scientific and technological information," welcoming both theoretical and empirical studies. The International Society for Scientometrics and Informetrics (ISSI) is an international association of scholars and professionals active in the interdisciplinary study of science, whose community focuses on quantitative approaches including informetrics, scientometrics, and webometrics.

label: Biochemistry
summary: Biochemistry is a discipline at the interface of chemistry and the life sciences. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as "the study of the chemical substances and processes that occur in plants, animals, and microorganisms and of the changes they undergo during development and life." Its dual character is visible in classification systems: the Library of Congress Classification files biochemistry under the hierarchy "Science--Chemistry--Organic chemistry--Biochemistry," while Britannica's own subject breadcrumb places the article under Science > Biology > Branches of Biology, and the Universal Decimal Classification lists "Material bases of life. Biochemistry. Molecular biology. Biophysics" under "Biological sciences in general." The American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology describes its community as "molecular life scientists" and frames its mission as advancing understanding of "the molecular nature of life processes," reflecting a field that draws co-equally on chemical methods and biological subject matter.

label: Bioethics
summary: Bioethics is the branch of applied ethics that studies the philosophical, social, and legal issues arising in medicine and the life sciences. It emerged as a distinct field of study in the early 1960s.

label: Bioinformatics
summary: Bioinformatics is an interdisciplinary field of science that develops computational methods and software tools for understanding biological data, especially when the data sets are large and complex. It synthesizes knowledge from biology, computer science, mathematics, and statistics to acquire, store, analyze, and interpret molecular information such as genome sequences, protein structures, and gene-expression measurements. Bioinformaticians build algorithms and databases for tasks including sequence alignment, genome assembly, structure prediction, and the modeling of biological networks. Though sometimes conflated with computational biology, which emphasizes mathematical modeling of biological systems, bioinformatics focuses on data-analysis methodologies. Within this atlas the field is homed in the life sciences, where it underpins genomics and molecular biology, and it is represented internationally by bodies such as the International Society for Computational Biology.

label: Biophysics
summary: Biophysics is a discipline at the interface of the physical and life sciences. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as a "discipline concerned with the application of the principles and methods of physics and the other physical sciences to the solution of biological problems," noting that biophysics and the closely related molecular biology "now are firmly established as cornerstones of modern biology." The Biophysical Society, the field's principal professional society, states its mission as "To lead an innovative global community working at the interface of the physical and life sciences, across all levels of complexity," reflecting a community that spans both parent domains rather than residing in one alone. Classification practice mirrors this dual character: the Universal Decimal Classification files biophysics under its life-sciences captions, listing "Material bases of life. Biochemistry. Molecular biology. Biophysics" within "Biological sciences in general," while physics communities study the same subject matter under headings such as the physics of living systems.

label: Biostatistics
summary: Biostatistics is a branch of statistics that applies statistical methods to a wide range of topics in the biological sciences, with a focus on clinical medicine and public health applications. The field encompasses the design of experiments, the collection and analysis of experimental and observational data, and the interpretation of the results. It is closely related to medical statistics.

label: Botany
summary: Botany, also called phytology or plant science, is the branch of natural science and biology that studies plants, especially their anatomy, taxonomy, and ecology. As a major subfield of biology, it spans the form, physiology, classification, distribution, and ecological relationships of plant life, from microscopic algae to flowering trees, alongside the practical uses of plants by humans. Botanical inquiry ranges across plant structure and development, reproduction, genetics, and the diversity of the plant kingdom. In the Library of Congress Classification, the literature of botany is gathered under class QK, organized from periodicals and societies through the systematic treatment of plant groups.

label: Buddhist Philosophy
summary: Buddhist philosophy encompasses the philosophical traditions that developed within or from Buddhism, originating with the teachings attributed to Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha), who lived in northern India between the mid-sixth and mid-fourth centuries BCE. Major traditions include Theravada, Madhyamaka, Yogacara, and Zen, which developed distinct philosophical positions on topics such as the nature of the self, consciousness, causation, and the path to liberation. Buddhist philosophy has been active across South, Southeast, East, and Central Asia, and continues as a living tradition studied in both religious and academic contexts.

label: Business Ethics
summary: Business ethics applies ethical theories and principles to the practices, institutions, and decisions of commerce and industry, including questions about corporate responsibility, fair dealing, labor rights, environmental obligations, and the ethics of advertising and finance. It overlaps with applied ethics, corporate governance, and law, and draws on normative theories including consequentialism, deontology, and stakeholder theory. The field gained academic recognition in the latter half of the twentieth century.

label: Calculus
summary: The branch of mathematics concerned with continuous change, built on derivatives and integrals.

label: Cardiology
summary: Cardiology is a branch of medicine that deals with disorders of the heart and the cardiovascular system, and it is a subspecialty of internal medicine. The field includes the medical diagnosis and treatment of conditions such as congenital heart defects, coronary artery disease, heart failure, and valvular heart disease.

label: Cardiothoracic Surgery
summary: Cardiothoracic surgery is the field of medicine involved in surgical treatment of organs inside the thoracic cavity, generally the heart, lungs, and other pleural or mediastinal structures. It is a surgical subspecialty addressing conditions of the chest.

label: Category Theory
summary: Category theory is the branch of mathematics that studies mathematical structures and the relationships between them through the unified language of categories, functors, and natural transformations. A category consists of a class of objects and a class of morphisms between them, closed under associative composition and equipped with identity morphisms; functors are structure-preserving maps between categories; and natural transformations are maps between functors. Category theory unifies constructions across algebra, topology, and logic by identifying universal properties shared by seemingly disparate mathematical objects.

label: Cell Biology
summary: Cell biology, also called cellular biology or cytology, is the branch of biology that studies the structure, function, and behavior of cells. The cell is the basic unit of life responsible for the living and functioning of an organism, and all organisms are made of cells. The discipline encompasses both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, with subtopics including cell metabolism, cell communication, the cell cycle, biochemistry, and cell composition. Cell biologists examine how organelles are organized, how cells divide and signal, and how molecular components sustain cellular life. The field connects molecular biology's account of macromolecules to the organized systems of whole cells, and serves as a forum for international research, exemplified by societies such as the American Society for Cell Biology.

label: Ceramic Arts
summary: Ceramic art, one of the plastic arts, is art made from ceramic materials, including clay. It may take forms such as pottery, tiles, figurines, sculptures, and tableware. While some ceramic products are considered fine art, others are considered decorative, industrial, or applied art objects; ceramics may also be considered artefacts in archaeology. People design, manufacture, and decorate pottery in pottery or ceramic factories, and in one-person pottery studios ceramists or potters produce studio pottery. Ceramics exclude glass and mosaics made from glass tesserae. As an artistic discipline and medium, ceramic art spans utilitarian and sculptural making, sitting within the decorative arts (LCC class NK) while overlapping the fine arts.

label: Chinese Philosophy
summary: Chinese philosophy encompasses the philosophical traditions that originated and developed in China, including Confucianism, Daoism, Legalism, Mohism, and later Buddhist-influenced schools. Its formative flourishing is associated with the Spring and Autumn (771–476 BCE) and Warring States periods, the era of the “Hundred Schools of Thought”. These traditions give particular weight to ethics, political philosophy, and cosmology.

label: Chiropractic
summary: Chiropractic is a form of alternative medicine concerned with the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of mechanical disorders of the musculoskeletal system, especially the spine. It is a licensed health care profession whose treatment typically involves manual therapy, often including spinal manipulation intended to improve joint motion and function. The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health and Wikipedia classify it among alternative-medicine practices.

label: Civil Law
summary: Civil law, in the branch-of-law sense, is the body of law governing non-criminal legal relationships between persons, as distinct from criminal law and from public law. Encyclopaedia Britannica characterizes private law, the broader category to which this branch belongs, as "private law regulating the actions, interests, and obligations of private persons." In the Universal Decimal Classification the branch is grouped under UDC 347, captioned "Civil law," whose own subdivisions enumerate its subject matter: 347.2 "Law of realty. Real rights" (property), 347.4 "Commitments. Contractual liabilities. Bonds. Contracts," 347.5 "Noncontractual liabilities. Torts," and 347.6 "Family law. Law of inheritance." UDC 347 sits alongside UDC 341 "International law," 342 "Public law. Constitutional law," and 343 "Criminal law" within the law class (UDC 34, "Law. Jurisprudence"). This referent is the substantive branch of private law, not a national or continental legal system.

label: Clinical Psychology
summary: Clinical psychology is, in the words of Wikipedia, "an integration of human science, behavioral science, theory, and clinical knowledge aimed at understanding, preventing, and relieving psychological distress or dysfunction as well as promoting well-being and personal growth." Central to its practice are "psychological assessment, diagnosis, clinical formulation, and psychotherapy." In many countries it is "a regulated mental health profession."

label: Cognitive Linguistics
summary: Cognitive linguistics is an approach to the study of language that encompasses a number of complementary and sometimes overlapping theories. Their defining characteristic is the guiding assumption that linguistic patterns are patterns of conceptualization, so that the study of language provides insight into other human cognitive functions. In this regard cognitive linguistics challenges generative grammar's hypothesis that some basic linguistic competence is innate and separate from other cognitive faculties.

label: Cognitive Neuroscience
summary: Cognitive neuroscience is the scientific field that is concerned with the study of the biological processes and aspects that underlie cognition, with a specific focus on the neural connections in the brain that are involved in mental processes. It is a branch of both neuroscience and psychology, and it relies upon theories in cognitive science coupled with evidence from neurobiology, and computational modeling.

label: Cognitive Psychology
summary: Cognitive psychology is "the scientific study of human mental processes such as attention, language use, memory, perception, problem solving, creativity, and reasoning." The field originated in the 1960s in a break from behaviorism, which had held that unobservable mental processes were outside the realm of empirical science. Work derived from cognitive psychology was later integrated into other branches of psychology and into disciplines such as cognitive science, linguistics, and economics.

label: Combinatorics
summary: Combinatorics is the branch of mathematics devoted to problems of selecting, arranging, and counting elements of finite or discrete systems according to prescribed rules. Its main areas include enumeration (counting configurations using permutations, combinations, and generating functions), design theory (studying block designs and Latin squares), and graph theory, which provides abstract models for relational structures and covers problems such as planar graphs, the four-colour map problem, and Eulerian cycles. Combinatorics has wide cross-connections with probability theory, algebra, number theory, and theoretical computer science.

label: Comparative Literature
summary: Comparative literature is the academic field dealing with the study of literature and cultural expression across linguistic, national, geographic, and disciplinary boundaries. It is most frequently practised with works of different languages, but may also compare works of the same language that originate from different nations or cultures.

label: Comparative Philosophy
summary: Comparative philosophy is the philosophical practice of examining and comparing concepts, arguments, and problems across distinct philosophical traditions, such as Chinese and Western philosophy.
