NIST describes it as a field that "marries two of the 20th century's most important scientific developments: quantum physics and information theory," and characterizes it as "using the smallest bits of matter and energy — electrons inside an atom, tiny circuits, massless particles of light — to store, carry and process information." The field is broader than quantum computing alone: NIST notes that while "scientists around the world are developing quantum computers," "other focus areas of quantum information science include quantum sensors for ultra-high-precision measurements and quantum networks that could link devices across cities, nations and ultimately the globe." The Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) taxonomy lists "Quantum Information, Science & Technology" as a discipline-level research area, spanning quantum computation, communication, and sensing.

label: Renaissance Philosophy
summary: Renaissance philosophy covers European philosophy from approximately the mid-15th to the early 17th century, a period marked by the recovery of the literary and philosophical classics of Greece and Rome and by the rise of humanism. Dominant currents include humanism, political philosophy, and the philosophy of nature, alongside Platonist revivals and renewed skepticism, often in opposition to Scholastic method. The period forms a transition between medieval and early modern philosophy.

label: Rhetoric
summary: Rhetoric is the art of persuasion, one of the three ancient arts of discourse (the trivium) of classical antiquity, along with grammar and logic/dialectic. As an academic discipline within the humanities, rhetoric aims to study the techniques that speakers or writers use to inform, persuade, and motivate their audiences.

label: Rheumatology
summary: Rheumatology is a branch of medicine devoted to the diagnosis and management of disorders whose common feature is inflammation in the bones, muscles, joints, and internal organs.

label: Robotics
summary: Robotics is the interdisciplinary study and practice of the design, construction, operation, and use of robots. It usually combines four aspects of design work: a power source, mechanical construction, a control system, and software, integrating mechanical, electrical, and computing engineering to build machines that can sense and act. The Library of Congress Classification places robots within range TJ210.2-TJ211.495, captioned "Mechanical devices and figures. Automata. Ingenious mechanisms. Robots (General)," which sits under the mechanical-engineering class TJ1-TJ1570. The IEEE Robotics and Automation Society, the field's principal professional body, states that "Robotics focuses on systems incorporating sensors and actuators that operate autonomously or semi-autonomously in cooperation with humans."

label: Scholasticism
summary: Scholasticism was the dominant method of philosophical and theological inquiry practiced in the medieval universities of Europe, characterized by systematic commentary on authoritative texts, formal disputation, and the reconciliation of reason with faith. Major scholastic philosophers include Anselm of Canterbury, Peter Abelard, Thomas Aquinas, Duns Scotus, and William of Ockham. The method left a lasting influence on Catholic theology and philosophy, and Thomism in particular experienced revivals into the twentieth century.

label: Scientific Computing
summary: Scientific computing, also called computational science, sits at the interface of computer science and applied mathematics, developing the algorithms, mathematical models, and high-performance computing techniques used to simulate problems across the sciences and engineering. Britannica’s entry defines computational science as applying “computer simulation, scientific visualization, mathematical modeling, algorithms, data structures, networking, database design, symbolic computation, and high-performance computing to help advance the goals of various disciplines.” Its interdisciplinary character is reflected in its scholarly homes: the Journal of Scientific Computing describes itself as “an international interdisciplinary forum for the publication of papers on state-of-the-art developments in scientific computing and its applications in science and engineering,” while SIAM’s Computational Science and Engineering activity group fosters “collaboration and interaction among applied mathematicians, computer scientists, domain scientists and engineers” and promotes simulation “as a mode of scientific discovery on the same level as theory and experiment.”

label: Sculpture
summary: Sculpture is the branch of the visual arts that operates in three dimensions, producing artwork physically presented in the dimensions of height, width, and depth. It is one of the plastic arts. Durable sculptural processes originally used carving and modelling—in stone, metal, ceramics, wood, and other materials—but since Modernism there has been almost complete freedom of materials and process. A wide variety of materials may be worked by removal such as carving, assembled by welding or modelling, or moulded or cast. In the Library of Congress Classification, sculpture forms class NB under Fine Arts, with periodicals and societies entered at the head of the range NB1–NB1952.

label: Seismology
summary: Seismology is the study of earthquakes and of the propagation of seismic waves through the Earth. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific discipline that is concerned with the study of earthquakes and of the propagation of seismic waves within the Earth," describing it as a branch of geophysics that has "provided much information about the composition and state of the planet's interior." The field uses recordings of seismic waves both to characterize earthquake sources and to probe the Earth's internal structure. Its scholarly community is institutionalized in bodies such as the Seismological Society of America, which presents its mission in terms of advancing "the science of seismology."

label: Semantics
summary: Semantics is the study of linguistic meaning, examining what meaning is, how words get their meaning, and how the meaning of a complex expression depends on its parts. Semantics contrasts with syntax, which studies the rules that dictate how to create grammatically correct sentences, and together with syntactics and pragmatics it is a part of semiotics.

label: Semiotics
summary: Semiotics is the study of signs, an interdisciplinary field that examines what signs are, how they form sign systems, and how individuals use them to communicate meaning. It is related to linguistics but has a broader scope that includes nonlinguistic signs, such as maps and clothing.

label: Sensation and Perception
summary: Sensation and perception is the area of psychology concerned with sensory processes, perception, attention, and psychophysics, classified in the APA PsycInfo classification under "Sensory Perception" (2320) and in the Library of Congress Classification under sensation (BF231-BF299). The field is served by dedicated journals such as Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, the official journal of the Psychonomic Society, which encompasses all areas of research in sensory processes, perception, attention, and psychophysics.

label: Set Theory
summary: Set theory is the branch of mathematical logic that studies well-defined collections of objects called sets, with particular focus on infinite sets and the foundations of mathematics. The standard axiom system, Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of Choice (ZFC), formalizes the theory and supports the development of ordinal and cardinal arithmetic, including the transfinite cardinals introduced by Georg Cantor. Central topics include forcing, the technique developed by Paul Cohen to prove independence results such as the independence of the Continuum Hypothesis from ZFC, and the study of large cardinal axioms that extend the standard system.

label: Social choice theory
summary: Social choice theory is a field at the intersection of economics, political science, and philosophy that studies how individual preferences, judgments, or welfare can be aggregated into a collective decision or social ranking. Its modern form was shaped by Kenneth Arrow, whose impossibility theorem showed that no aggregation rule can simultaneously satisfy a set of apparently reasonable fairness conditions, and by later work associated with Amartya Sen and others on welfare, rights, and measurement. The field encompasses voting theory, welfare economics, and the analysis of fairness and collective rationality, and has close ties to game theory and to normative debates about democracy and distributive justice.

label: Social Computing
summary: Social computing is the area of computer science that studies the design and use of computational systems and technologies in relation to social behavior, interaction, and organizations. The ACM Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work and Social Computing (CSCW) is described as "the premier venue for research in the design and use of technologies that affect groups, organizations, communities, and networks," exploring "the technical, social, material, and theoretical challenges of designing technology to support collaborative work and life activities." Its 29th edition, CSCW 2026, is scheduled for Salt Lake City, Utah, in October 2026.

label: Social History
summary: Social history, often called history from below, is the field of history that looks at the lived experience of the past. Historians who write social history are called social historians.

label: Social Philosophy
summary: Social philosophy is the philosophical study of society and its institutions, approached in terms of ethical values rather than empirical relations. It emphasizes understanding the social contexts of political, legal, moral, and cultural questions, and develops theoretical frameworks ranging from social ontology and care ethics to cosmopolitan theories of democracy, natural law, human rights, gender equity, and global justice. Its questions overlap considerably with those of ethics and value theory, and it is broadly interdisciplinary, examining areas such as phenomenology, epistemology, and philosophy of language from a sociological perspective. Following a distinction drawn by Leo Strauss, social philosophy is distinguished from political philosophy in that it approaches largely the same subject matter from the broader vantage of “society”.

label: Social Psychology
summary: Social psychology is "the methodical study of how thoughts, feelings, and behaviors are influenced by the actual, imagined, or implied presence of others." Britannica describes it as "the scientific study of the behaviour of individuals in their social and cultural setting," with the emphasis on human social behaviour. It is a branch of psychology concerned with how the social context shapes individual mental life and conduct.

label: Social Stratification
summary: Social stratification is the study of structured inequalities between groups in society and of movement among social positions. It is a core area of sociology: in the Universal Decimal Classification, sociology occupies class 316 "Sociology," within which 316.3 is captioned "Social structure. Society as a social system." The field's principal international scholarly body is the Research Committee on Social Stratification and Mobility (RC28) of the International Sociological Association, whose page notes that "Research in Social Stratification and Mobility is the official journal of the ISA RC28." The committee's sustained focus on stratification and mobility situates the subfield within sociology's broader analysis of social structure.

label: Social Work and Welfare
summary: Social work is both an academic discipline and a profession concerned with human well-being and social welfare. The Global Definition of the Social Work Profession, approved by the International Federation of Social Workers (IFSW) and the International Association of Schools of Social Work in July 2014, states: "Social work is a practice-based profession and an academic discipline that promotes social change and development, social cohesion, and the empowerment and liberation of people." The U.S. National Association of Social Workers characterizes it in practice terms, noting that "Social workers assist people by helping them cope with issues in their everyday lives, deal with their relationships, and solve personal and family problems." In the Universal Decimal Classification the area is grouped under class 36, "Safeguarding the mental and material necessities of life," which includes social work and the welfare subdivision 364 "Social welfare."

label: Sociolinguistics
summary: Sociolinguistics is the descriptive and scientific study of how language is shaped by and used differently within any given society. The field looks at how a language varies between distinct social groups and under the influence of assorted cultural norms, expectations, and contexts. It combines the older field of dialectology with the social sciences in order to identify regional dialects, sociolects, and other sub-varieties within a language.

label: Soft Matter Physics
summary: Soft matter physics studies materials that are readily deformed by thermal fluctuations or modest external stresses, including colloids, polymers, gels, foams, and biological and granular matter. The American Physical Society's Division of Soft Matter describes soft matter as "a broad class of physical states ranging from colloids and micelles to biological and granular matter that are easily deformed by external stresses," adding that "The common feature of these materials is that the predominant physical behaviors occur at energy scales comparable with thermal energy." Its stated mission is to "advance knowledge and build community among the interdisciplinary group of scientists, mathematicians, and engineers working on soft matter physics." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society it appears within the discipline "Polymers & Soft Matter."

label: Software Engineering
summary: Software engineering is the discipline concerned with the systematic application of engineering principles to the specification, design, development, testing, and maintenance of software systems. Britannica defines it as "the discipline concerned with the application of theory, knowledge, and practice to building reliable software systems that satisfy the computing requirements of customers and users," applicable to small-, medium-, and large-scale systems. Britannica also notes that Margaret Hamilton is credited with creating the term "software engineer" to describe her professional work, which included writing code for the command and lunar modules of NASA's Apollo program in the late 1960s and early 1970s. ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM), publishing since 1992, covers "specification, design, development and maintenance" and the tools, methodologies, languages, data structures, and algorithms involved in building large, complex software systems.

label: Special Education
summary: Special education is the field concerned with the education of children whose needs differ from the typical to a degree requiring adapted instruction. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as "the education of children who differ socially, mentally, or physically from the average to such an extent that they require modifications of usual school practices," serving "children with emotional, behavioral, or cognitive impairments or with intellectual, hearing, vision, speech, or learning disabilities; gifted children with advanced academic abilities; and children with orthopedic or neurological impairments." The principal learned body in the field, the Council for Exceptional Children (CEC), describes itself as a "professional organization dedicated to improving the success of children and youth with disabilities and/or gifts and talents." In the Universal Decimal Classification the field is grouped under UDC 376, "Education, teaching, training of special groups of persons. Special schools."

label: Statistical Physics and Thermodynamics
summary: Statistical physics applies statistical methods to systems of many constituents in order to derive their macroscopic properties from the behavior of their microscopic parts. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines statistical mechanics—a core component—as the "branch of physics that combines the principles and procedures of statistics with the laws of both classical and quantum mechanics, particularly with respect to the field of thermodynamics," noting that "It aims to predict and explain the measurable properties of macroscopic systems" from their microscopic constituents. The related discipline of thermodynamics is defined by Britannica as the "science of the relationship between heat, work, temperature, and energy." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society the field appears as the discipline "Statistical Physics & Thermodynamics."

label: Structural anthropology
summary: Structural anthropology is an approach in anthropology, most closely associated with Claude Lévi-Strauss, that analyzes culture as a system of underlying structures modeled on the relational and binary logic of structural linguistics. It holds that phenomena such as myth, kinship, and classification can be understood as expressions of universal patterns of the human mind, particularly binary oppositions and their transformations. Developed principally in the mid-twentieth century, it drew on the linguistics of Ferdinand de Saussure and Roman Jakobson and was highly influential across the social sciences and humanities before being challenged by post-structuralist and other later critiques.

label: Structural Engineering
summary: Structural engineering is a sub-discipline of civil engineering concerned with the analysis and design of structures that must safely support or resist loads. Wikipedia characterizes it as the field "in which structural engineers are trained to design the 'bones and joints' that create the form and shape of human-made structures," adding that engineers "must understand and calculate the stability, strength, rigidity and earthquake-susceptibility of built structures for buildings and nonbuilding structures." The discipline rests on applied physical laws and empirical knowledge of how different materials and geometries perform under stress. Typical work covers buildings, bridges, towers, and other load-bearing systems, ensuring they withstand gravity, wind, seismic, and service loads. The Library of Congress Classification gives structural engineering its own heading, "Structural engineering (General)," within the broader civil engineering range.

label: Syntax
summary: In linguistics, syntax is the study of how words and morphemes combine to form well-formed larger units such as phrases and sentences. Central concerns in this area of linguistics include word order, grammatical relations, hierarchical sentence structure, agreement, and cross-linguistic variation. Diverse approaches, such as generative grammar and functional grammar, offer unique perspectives on syntax.

label: Systematic Theology
summary: Systematic theology is a discipline of Christian theology that formulates an orderly, rational, and coherent account of the doctrines of the Christian faith. It addresses issues such as what the Bible teaches about certain topics, and it shares its systematic tasks with other disciplines such as constructive theology, dogmatics, ethics, and apologetics.

label: Systematics
summary: Systematics is the study of the diversification of living forms, both past and present, and the relationships among living things through time. Encompassing taxonomy and phylogenetics, it reconstructs evolutionary trees to represent the branching order and divergence of lineages, and uses these phylogenies to examine trait evolution and the geographic distribution of organisms. The Society of Systematic Biologists describes its mission as advancing the science of systematic biology in all its aspects of theory, principles, methodology, and practice, for both living and fossil organisms. In the Library of Congress Classification, the work of classification and nomenclature falls within natural history in class QH.

label: Systems Engineering
summary: Systems engineering is an interdisciplinary field of engineering and engineering management that focuses on how to design, integrate, and manage complex systems over their life cycles. It uses systems-thinking principles to organize the systems engineering body of knowledge, and the resulting engineered system can be defined as a combination of components that work in synergy to collectively perform a useful function. Rather than optimizing parts in isolation, the discipline coordinates requirements, architecture, interfaces, verification, and operations across a system's whole life cycle, from concept through retirement. The international professional society for the discipline is the International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE).

label: Systems Neuroscience
summary: Systems neuroscience is a subdiscipline of neuroscience and systems biology that studies the structure and function of various neural circuits and systems that make up the central nervous system of an organism. It is concerned with how nerve cells behave when connected together to form neural pathways, neural circuits, and larger brain networks, addressing how such circuits analyze sensory information, form perceptions, and execute movements.

label: Telecommunications Engineering
summary: Telecommunications engineering is a subfield of electrical engineering which seeks to design and devise systems of communication at a distance. The work ranges from basic circuit design to strategic mass developments. A telecommunication engineer is responsible for designing and overseeing the installation of telecommunications equipment and facilities, such as complex electronic switching systems, optical fiber cabling, IP networks, and microwave transmission systems. The discipline also overlaps with broadcast engineering. Its subject matter—telephony, radio, fiber-optic and IP networks, and spectrum use—is coordinated internationally by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), described as "the United Nations specialized agency for digital technologies (ICTs)."

label: Textile Engineering
summary: Textile engineering, also termed textile manufacturing, is the engineering discipline concerned with the production and processing of textiles. It is largely based on the conversion of fibre into yarn, then yarn into fabric. These are then dyed or printed and fabricated into cloth, which is converted into useful goods such as clothing, household items, upholstery, and various industrial products. The discipline thus spans fibre science, yarn spinning, fabric formation, and finishing operations including dyeing and printing. The Library of Congress classifies textile industries at TS1300 and above, under "Technology--Manufactures--Textile industries." The Textile Institute, founded in Manchester in 1910, is "the professional body for people and organisations working in the textile, clothing and footwear associated industries worldwide."

label: Theatre Studies
summary: Theatre studies is the academic study of theatrical performance in relation to its literary, physical, psychological, sociological, and historical contexts. It is an interdisciplinary field which also encompasses the study of theatrical aesthetics and semiotics, examining not only dramatic texts but also acting, staging, design, audience reception, and the institutions and cultures of performance. The discipline draws on dramatic literature, performance theory, theatre history, and the practical analysis of production, distinguishing the scholarly study of theatre from its professional practice. In the Library of Congress Classification, dramatic and theatrical performance is classed in the range PN2000-PN3307, "Dramatic representation. The theater," within the Language and Literature schedule, reflecting the field's historical roots in the study of drama as a literary and performance form.

label: Theology
summary: Theology is the study of religious belief from a religious perspective, with a focus on the nature of divinity and the history behind religion. It is taught as an academic discipline, typically in universities and seminaries.

label: Theoretical Computer Science
summary: Theoretical computer science (TCS) is the branch of computer science concerned with the formal analysis of efficient computation and computational processes. The ACM Special Interest Group on Algorithms and Computation Theory (SIGACT) characterizes TCS as covering "algorithms, data structures, computational complexity, parallel and distributed computation, probabilistic computation, quantum computation, automata theory, information theory, cryptography, program semantics and verification, machine learning, computational biology, computational economics, computational geometry, and computational number theory and algebra," with work in the field distinguished by its emphasis on mathematical technique and rigor. SIGACT itself is described as an international organization that "fosters and promotes the discovery and dissemination of high quality research in theoretical computer science." Among the conferences SIGACT sponsors are STOC and ITCS, with in-cooperation venues including SODA and FOCS.

label: Thermodynamics
summary: Thermodynamics is the branch of physics that examines how heat and work move energy through physical systems, and how that exchange constrains matter and radiation through the related concept of entropy. Four governing laws describe these exchanges in measurable, macroscopic terms, while statistical mechanics supplies a microscopic account of the same behavior. The field took shape in the early nineteenth century out of efforts to improve the efficiency of steam engines, with Sadi Carnot's 1824 analysis of engine efficiency an early landmark; Rudolf Clausius introduced the term entropy in 1865 while working out the second law. The field now comprises several distinct branches — including chemical, equilibrium, non-equilibrium, classical, and statistical thermodynamics — each built on a different model or applied to a different class of system.

label: Time Series Analysis
summary: Time series analysis is the branch of statistics concerned with data observed sequentially over time, formally treating such data as realizations of stochastic processes. Core methods include the analysis of stationary processes, spectral decomposition, moving-average models, and forecasting; Robert F. Engle and Clive W. J. Granger developed influential techniques for series exhibiting time-varying volatility and common trends respectively. The field finds application across economics, engineering, meteorology, and the natural sciences wherever measurements are ordered in time.

label: Topology
summary: Topology is the branch of mathematics that studies properties of spaces preserved under continuous deformations — transformations such as bending, twisting, and stretching that do not involve tearing or gluing. It divides into two principal sub-disciplines: general (or point-set) topology, which investigates abstract topological spaces, continuity, compactness, and connectedness; and algebraic topology, which assigns algebraic invariants such as fundamental groups and homology groups to spaces in order to classify them. Differential topology and knot theory are among the other major areas within the field.

label: Toxicology
summary: Toxicology is a scientific discipline, overlapping with biology, chemistry, pharmacology, and medicine, that involves the study of the adverse effects of chemical substances on living organisms. The relationship between dose and its effects on the exposed organism is of high significance in the field. Factors that influence chemical toxicity include the dosage, duration of exposure, route of exposure, species, age, sex, and environment.

label: Translation Studies
summary: Translation studies is an academic interdiscipline dealing with the systematic study of the theory, description and application of translation, interpreting, and localization. As an interdiscipline it borrows from supporting fields including comparative literature, computer science, history, linguistics, philology, philosophy, semiotics, and terminology.

label: Transportation Engineering
summary: Transportation engineering is the sub-discipline of civil engineering that applies scientific and engineering principles to the planning, design, operation, and management of transportation systems. Wikipedia defines it as "the application of technology and scientific principles to the planning, functional design, operation and management of facilities for any mode of transportation to provide for the safe, efficient, rapid, comfortable, convenient, economical, and environmentally compatible movement of people and goods." The field spans highway, rail, transit, air, water, and pipeline modes. ASCE's Transportation & Development Institute, established in 2002, is dedicated to "advancing knowledge and practice in sustainable transportation and development." The Library of Congress Classification recognizes the discipline under the heading "Transportation engineering" within civil engineering. Work ranges from traffic and pavement design to network operations and infrastructure planning.

label: Type theory
summary: In mathematical logic and theoretical computer science, type theory studies formal systems that sort expressions and mathematical objects into types, with each type restricting how an expression may be formed and used, in a way loosely comparable to how a data type constrains values in a programming language. Bertrand Russell worked out the approach between 1902 and 1908 to avoid paradoxes such as the one bearing his name in naive set theory, arriving by 1908 at a hierarchy of types paired with a reducibility axiom, both later formalized in his and Alfred North Whitehead's Principia Mathematica (1910–1913). In the twentieth century the field developed alongside Alonzo Church's lambda calculus and now includes systems such as Per Martin-Löf's intuitionistic type theory, which supports a constructive approach to mathematical foundations, and Thierry Coquand's calculus of constructions, which underlies proof assistants including Rocq (formerly Coq) and Lean.

label: Urban and Regional Planning
summary: Urban and regional planning, also called spatial planning, is the management of space and resources through the creation and implementation of plans restricting how space can be used and developed. Normally undertaken by state actors at national, regional, or local levels, it tries to balance the competing demands upon land as a resource, mediating between the demands of the state, market, and local community. The field has a dual disciplinary home. The Library of Congress Classification files city planning both under the social sciences as "City planning" within urban sociology (HT165.5-HT169.9) and under fine arts/architecture as "Aesthetics of cities. City planning and beautifying" (NA9000-NA9428); the ANZSRC classification places it within Built Environment and Design. It is thus framed as a social-science discipline of regional and spatial organization with an equally grounded home in the design tradition.

label: Urban Planning
summary: Urban planning is the process of developing and designing plans for land use and the built environment, including the air, water, and infrastructure passing into and out of urban areas, such as transportation, communications, and distribution networks. A narrower, city-scale subclass of spatial planning, it has historically concerned itself with public welfare, efficiency, sanitation, and the protection and use of the environment, more recently emphasizing health, well-being, and sustainability. The discipline carries a dual character. The Library of Congress Classification maps city planning to architecture ("Aesthetics of cities. City planning and beautifying," NA9000-NA9428) and to urban sociology ("City planning," HT165.5-HT169.9); Wikidata describes it as a "technical and political process concerned with the use of land and design of the urban environment." Its atlas home is architecture and the arts, cross-listed into social policy and public administration.

label: Urology
summary: Urology, also known as genitourinary surgery, is the branch of medicine that focuses on surgical and medical diseases of the urinary system and the male reproductive organs. Organs under its domain include the kidneys, adrenal glands, ureters, urinary bladder, urethra, and the male reproductive organs.

label: Virology
summary: Virology is the scientific study of biological viruses. It is a subfield of microbiology that focuses on their detection, structure, classification and evolution, their methods of infection and exploitation of host cells for reproduction, their interaction with host organism physiology and immunity, the diseases they cause, the techniques to isolate and culture them, and their use in research and therapy. Virological inquiry spans both the molecular biology of viral replication and the epidemiology of viral disease. In the Library of Congress Classification, the literature of virology is placed under microbiology in class QR.

label: Visualization
summary: Visualization (in computing) is the study and practice of transforming data into visual representations to support tasks ranging from rapid observation to in-depth analysis. The IEEE VIS conference—the field's primary venue—defines visualization as "the study of the transformation of data to visual representations, which provide cost-effective means for supporting a variety of data intelligence tasks," and describes it as having expanded to encompass scientific visualization, information visualization, and visual analytics. IEEE VIS organizes research across areas including theoretical and empirical work, visualization systems and rendering, data transformations, and visual analytics for decision-making.

label: Volcanology
summary: Volcanology is the branch of the geologic sciences concerned with volcanoes and volcanic phenomena. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "discipline of the geologic sciences that is concerned with all aspects of volcanic phenomena," addressing "the formation, distribution, and classification of volcanoes as well as with their structure and the kinds of materials ejected during an eruption." The field studies how volcanoes form and are distributed, the products of eruptions, and the processes that drive volcanic activity. In the Library of Congress Classification, volcanoes are treated alongside earthquakes in the range QE521-QE545, labeled "Volcanoes and earthquakes," within the geology subclass QE.

label: World History
summary: World history, or global history, is the field of historical study that examines history from a global perspective. It emerged centuries ago and became much more active as a field in the late 20th century.

label: Zoology
summary: Zoology is the scientific study of animals, including the structure, embryology, classification, habits, and distribution of all animals, both living and extinct, and how they interact with their ecosystems. It is one of the primary branches of biology, with the term derived from Ancient Greek zoion, 'animal,' and logos, 'study of.' As a subfield, zoology encompasses animal morphology and physiology, behavior, evolutionary relationships, and the diversity of the animal kingdom across taxonomic groups. In the Library of Congress Classification, the literature of zoology is collected under class QL, organized from periodicals and societies through the systematic treatment of animal taxa.

label: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
summary: "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" is a 1948 paper by Claude Shannon, published in the Bell System Technical Journal, that founded the field of information theory. It introduced a quantitative measure of information (entropy), the modeling of communication sources and channels, and results on the fundamental limits of data compression and reliable transmission over noisy channels. It is widely regarded as the canonical work establishing information theory and is foundational to modern communications, computing, and data science.

label: The Laws of Thought
summary: An Investigation of the Laws of Thought is a book by the English mathematician George Boole, published in 1854. It developed an algebraic treatment of logic in which logical reasoning is expressed through symbolic operations, laying the groundwork for what is now known as Boolean algebra. It is a founding work of modern symbolic and mathematical logic.
aliases: An Investigation of the Laws of Thought

label: Begriffsschrift
summary: Begriffsschrift (Concept-Script) is a short book by the German mathematician and philosopher Gottlob Frege, published in 1879, that introduced a formal notation for a logic of quantifiers and variables. It presented the first system of modern predicate (quantificational) logic, superseding the term logic inherited from Aristotle. It is a foundational work in modern logic and analytic philosophy.

label: Capital, Volume I
summary: Capital, Volume I (German: Das Kapital, Volume I) is an 1867 work of political economy by Karl Marx, the first and only volume he published in his lifetime; the later volumes were edited from his manuscripts and published after his death. It presents a critical analysis of capitalist production, developing Marx's account of the commodity, value, and the extraction of surplus value from labor. It is widely regarded as a foundational text of Marxist thought and has been highly influential across economics and the social sciences, including sociology.

label: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
summary: "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" is a paper written by Alan Turing on the topic of artificial intelligence, published in 1950 in Mind. It was the first to introduce his concept of what is now known as the Turing test to the general public. The paper considers the question "Can machines think?" and, holding that the words "think" and "machine" cannot clearly be defined, proposes to replace the question with a closely related one expressed in relatively unambiguous words, substituting a simple, unambiguous concept for the term "think."

label: Cours de linguistique générale
summary: Cours de linguistique générale ("Course in General Linguistics") is a foundational work of modern linguistics, compiled by students from lecture notes and published in 1916, after his death, under the name of the Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure. It sets out key distinctions such as langue and parole, the synchronic and diachronic study of language, and the arbitrary nature of the linguistic sign, treating language as a system of signs. It is widely regarded as a founding text of structural linguistics and a major influence on structuralism across the humanities.

label: Cours de philosophie positive
summary: Cours de philosophie positive (Course in Positive Philosophy) is a work by the French philosopher Auguste Comte, published in six volumes between 1830 and 1842. It set out his doctrine of positivism, including the law of three stages and a classification of the sciences, and proposed a positive science of society for which he coined the term sociology. It is a founding work of positivism and of sociology.

label: Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine
summary: Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine is a book by the American mathematician Norbert Wiener, first published in 1948. It proposed a unified study of control, feedback, and communication in living organisms and machines, drawing together ideas from engineering, neuroscience, and statistics. The book named and founded the field of cybernetics.

label: De humani corporis fabrica
summary: De humani corporis fabrica (On the Fabric of the Human Body) is an illustrated treatise on human anatomy by the Flemish physician Andreas Vesalius, published in 1543. Based on Vesalius's own dissections, it corrected numerous long-standing errors inherited from Galen and set a new standard for anatomical observation and illustration. It is widely regarded as a founding work of modern anatomy.
aliases: De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem

label: Experiments on Plant Hybridization
summary: Experiments on Plant Hybridization (Versuche uber Pflanzen-Hybriden) is a paper by the monk and naturalist Gregor Mendel, presented in 1865 and published in 1866, reporting his breeding experiments with pea plants. From patterns of inheritance across generations it inferred the discrete factors and segregation rules now known as Mendelian inheritance. Largely overlooked at the time, it became foundational to genetics after its rediscovery around 1900.

label: Grundlagen einer allgemeinen Mannigfaltigkeitslehre
summary: Grundlagen einer allgemeinen Mannigfaltigkeitslehre (Foundations of a General Theory of Manifolds) is a monograph by the German mathematician Georg Cantor, published in 1883. It systematically developed the theory of transfinite numbers and the treatment of infinite sets, defending the actual infinite as a legitimate mathematical object. It is a foundational work in the development of set theory.
aliases: Foundations of a General Theory of Aggregates

label: Logical Investigations
summary: Logical Investigations (Logische Untersuchungen) is a work by the German philosopher Edmund Husserl, published in two parts in 1900-1901. It criticized psychologism in logic and developed detailed analyses of meaning, intentionality, and the structure of experience. It is a founding work of the phenomenological movement.

label: On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem
summary: "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem" is a 1936 paper by Alan Turing that introduces the abstract computing device now known as the Turing machine and defines the notion of a computable number. Using this framework, Turing showed that certain problems, including the decision problem (Entscheidungsproblem) for first-order logic, cannot be solved by any such machine. It is widely regarded as a founding paper of computability theory and theoretical computer science.

label: On Crimes and Punishments
summary: On Crimes and Punishments (Dei delitti e delle pene) is a treatise by the Italian jurist and philosopher Cesare Beccaria, published in 1764. It criticized arbitrary and cruel punishment, argued against torture and the death penalty, and held that penalties should be proportionate, prompt, and fixed by law to deter crime. It is a founding work of modern criminology and of classical liberal penal reform.

label: On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems
summary: "On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems I" (German: "Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze der Principia Mathematica und verwandter Systeme I") is a paper in mathematical logic by Kurt Gödel. Submitted November 17, 1930, it was originally published in German in the 1931 volume of Monatshefte für Mathematik und Physik. The paper contains Gödel's incompleteness theorems, now fundamental results in logic that have many implications for consistency proofs in mathematics, and is also known for introducing new techniques that Gödel invented to prove the incompleteness theorems.

label: On Sense and Reference
summary: In the philosophy of language, the distinction between sense and reference was an idea of the German philosopher and mathematician Gottlob Frege in 1892, in his paper "On Sense and Reference" (German: "Über Sinn und Bedeutung"), reflecting the two ways he believed a singular term may have meaning. The reference (Bedeutung) of a proper name is the object it means or indicates, whereas its sense (Sinn) is what the name expresses. Frege held that sense is something possessed by a name whether or not it has a reference, and that different names may have the same reference but different senses. Much of analytic philosophy is traceable to Frege's philosophy of language.

label: On the Origin of Species
summary: On the Origin of Species is an 1859 book by Charles Darwin that presents the theory of evolution by natural selection, arguing that species descend with modification from common ancestors and that natural selection is a principal mechanism driving this change. Marshalling extensive evidence from natural history, breeding, and biogeography, it is widely regarded as one of the foundational and most influential works of modern biology and as the canonical text establishing evolutionary biology.

label: Opticks
summary: Opticks: or, A Treatise of the Reflexions, Refractions, Inflexions and Colours of Light is a collection of three books by Isaac Newton that was published in English in 1704, with a scholarly Latin translation appearing in 1706. The treatise analyses the fundamental nature of light by means of the refraction of light with prisms and lenses, the diffraction of light by closely spaced sheets of glass, and the behaviour of colour mixtures with spectral lights or pigment powders. Opticks was Newton's second major work on physical science and is considered one of the three major works on optics during the Scientific Revolution, alongside Johannes Kepler's Astronomiae Pars Optica and Christiaan Huygens' Treatise on Light.

label: Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica
summary: Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica ("Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy"), commonly called the Principia, is a work by Isaac Newton first published in 1687 that sets out his laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation. Written in Latin and using geometrical methods, it provides a unified mathematical account of terrestrial and celestial motion and is widely regarded as one of the most important works in the history of science and a foundational text of classical physics.
aliases: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy

label: Principles of Geology
summary: Principles of Geology is a work by the Scottish geologist Charles Lyell, published in three volumes between 1830 and 1833, that argued Earth's features are the product of gradual, ongoing natural processes acting over immense periods of time. It gave systematic form to the doctrine of uniformitarianism, holding that the same causes observable today have operated throughout geological history. The book was highly influential on nineteenth-century earth science and on Charles Darwin's thinking about deep time.

label: Principles of Physiological Psychology
summary: Principles of Physiological Psychology (Grundzuge der physiologischen Psychologie) is a work by the German scientist Wilhelm Wundt, first published in 1873-1874. It set out a program for treating psychology as an experimental science grounded in physiology and the study of immediate conscious experience. It is regarded as a founding text of experimental psychology.

label: Social Choice and Individual Values
summary: Social Choice and Individual Values is a book by the American economist Kenneth Arrow, first published in 1951. It gave a formal analysis of aggregating individual preferences into a collective ranking and proved Arrow's impossibility theorem, showing that no aggregation rule can simultaneously satisfy a small set of reasonable fairness conditions. It is a founding work of modern social choice theory.

label: Structural Anthropology
summary: Structural Anthropology (Anthropologie structurale) is a collection of essays by the French anthropologist Claude Levi-Strauss, first published in 1958. It applied models drawn from structural linguistics to kinship, myth, and social organization, arguing that cultural phenomena can be analyzed as systems of underlying relations. It is a foundational work of structuralist anthropology.

label: Syntactic Structures
summary: Syntactic Structures is a short book by the linguist Noam Chomsky, published in 1957. It introduced a formal, generative approach to grammar in which a finite set of rules generates the sentences of a language, and argued for transformational rules relating sentence structures. It is widely regarded as a founding work of generative grammar and a catalyst of modern theoretical linguistics.

label: Systema Naturae
summary: Systema Naturae is a work by the Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus, first published in 1735 and expanded through many later editions, that set out a hierarchical classification of the natural world into kingdoms, classes, orders, genera, and species. Its tenth edition (1758) is taken as the starting point for the modern system of binomial nomenclature for animals. It is a foundational work of biological taxonomy.

label: The Interpretation of Dreams
summary: The Interpretation of Dreams (German: Die Traumdeutung) is a book by Sigmund Freud, published in 1899 and dated 1900, that presents his theory that dreams are disguised fulfillments of unconscious wishes and can be analyzed to reveal repressed mental content. It introduces influential concepts such as the distinction between the manifest and latent content of dreams and the mechanisms of dream-work, and lays out central ideas of psychoanalysis. It is widely regarded as one of Freud's foundational works and a canonical text of psychoanalysis.

label: The Mind of Primitive Man
summary: The Mind of Primitive Man is a book by the German-American anthropologist Franz Boas, first published in 1911. It argued against ranking human groups on a single evolutionary scale and against equating race, language, and culture, holding that cultural differences reflect history and environment rather than innate biological capacity. It is a foundational statement of cultural relativism in modern anthropology.

label: The Problems of Philosophy
summary: The Problems of Philosophy is a book by the British philosopher Bertrand Russell, published in 1912. Written as a concise introduction, it examines questions about knowledge, perception, the existence of matter, universals, and the distinction between knowledge by acquaintance and knowledge by description. It is widely used as a classic introductory text in the analytic tradition.

label: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
summary: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (Die protestantische Ethik und der Geist des Kapitalismus) is a work by the German sociologist Max Weber, published as essays in 1904-1905. It argued that ascetic Protestantism, especially Calvinist ideas about vocation and worldly discipline, contributed to the cultural attitudes that fostered modern capitalism. It is a landmark work in the sociology of religion and of economic life.
aliases: Die protestantische Ethik und der Geist des Kapitalismus

label: The Rules of Sociological Method
summary: The Rules of Sociological Method (Les Regles de la methode sociologique) is a book by the French sociologist Emile Durkheim, published in 1895. It argued that sociology has a distinct subject matter of social facts, which are to be treated as external, constraining realities and studied objectively "as things." It is a founding methodological statement of sociology as an autonomous science.
aliases: Les Règles de la méthode sociologique

label: The Social Stratification of English in New York City
summary: The Social Stratification of English in New York City is a study by the linguist William Labov, first published in 1966 and based on his doctoral research. Using systematic recorded interviews, it demonstrated that variation in features such as postvocalic "r" correlates with social class and speech style, showing that linguistic variation is socially structured and quantifiable. It is a foundational work of variationist sociolinguistics.

label: The Wealth of Nations
summary: The Wealth of Nations, full title An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, is a 1776 work by the Scottish philosopher and economist Adam Smith. It analyzes how national wealth arises from the division of labor, productive labor, and markets coordinated through self-interested exchange, and argues broadly in favor of free trade and limited government intervention. It is widely regarded as a foundational text of modern economics and as the canonical work marking the emergence of the discipline as a systematic field of study.
aliases: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations

label: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior
summary: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, published in 1944 by Princeton University Press, is a book by mathematician John von Neumann and economist Oskar Morgenstern which is considered the groundbreaking text that created the interdisciplinary research field of game theory. In its introduction to the 60th anniversary edition, Princeton University Press describes the book as "the classic work upon which modern-day game theory is based."

label: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
summary: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus is a philosophical work by Ludwig Wittgenstein, first published in German in 1921 and in English translation in 1922. Written as a series of numbered propositions, it advances a picture theory of meaning and analyzes the relationship between language, thought, and the world, culminating in claims about the limits of what can be meaningfully said. It is widely regarded as a major work of analytic philosophy and a canonical text in the philosophy of language and logic.

label: Traité élémentaire de chimie
summary: Traite elementaire de chimie (Elementary Treatise on Chemistry) is a textbook by the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier, published in 1789, that presented chemistry on the basis of careful quantitative measurement and the law of conservation of mass. It introduced a reformed chemical nomenclature and a list of elements defined as substances not decomposable by then-available means, rejecting the phlogiston theory. It is regarded as a founding text of modern chemistry.
